title: Ali 'Imran
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
Āl ʿImrān, the third surah of the Qur’an, was revealed in Madinah and has 200 verses. Its name means “the family of Imran,” and one of its major passages tells of Maryam (Mary), her family, and the birth and mission of ʿĪsā (Jesus). The surah brings questions of belief into conversation with history and public life. It calls people to worship Allah alone, recognize the continuity of revelation, and remain faithful when belief is tested by argument, prosperity, conflict, or loss.

### How it follows Al-Baqarah

Al-Fatihah ends with a prayer for guidance. Al-Baqarah answers by presenting the Qur’an as guidance, then sets out teachings and duties and describes opposition to the believers. Its closing prayer asks Allah for help against those who reject faith. Āl ʿImrān continues that concern. It addresses how believers should engage with those who reject the message and describes striving for Allah’s cause in word and action. The two surahs thus connect the request for guidance with the work of holding to it and calling others toward it.

### When it was revealed

The surah is Madinan. The opening eighty-three verses are linked in the material to a delegation from Najran that came to Madinah in the ninth year after the Hijrah, identified there as 632 CE. The later passage about the call to settle a dispute concerning ʿĪsā is connected with that setting (3:61). The surah’s discussion of earlier prophets and revelation also places its message within a long history of calls to worship Allah alone.

### What the surah covers

The opening establishes Allah’s oneness, knowledge, power, and authority, then distinguishes between verses whose meaning is clear and those that call for humility rather than speculation. It warns against rejecting revelation and against mistaking worldly wealth or status for lasting success. It recalls past communities and the consequences of denying messengers, while presenting divine support and accountability as central lessons of history.

A substantial part of the surah tells the story of Maryam and her family, including her mother’s dedication, the care of Zakariyya, and the announcement and birth of Yahya (John) and ʿĪsā. It describes ʿĪsā’s mission, signs, disciples, and deliverance from a plot against him. These passages challenge claims about his status by comparing him with Adam and inviting a fair resolution of disagreement. The surah also calls the People of the Book and the wider community to common ground: worship Allah alone and do not give partners to Him. It affirms the shared message of the prophets, including Ibrāhīm (Abraham), and the duty to believe in all of them.

The surah then turns to the believers’ own conduct. It teaches unity, warns against harmful alliances and influences, calls for generosity and justice, and sets out the duty of pilgrimage. Its extended account of the battle of Uhud faces the pain of setback directly. It considers the choices and failures that led to loss, the Prophet’s leadership, forgiveness, steadfastness, and the honor given to those killed in Allah’s cause. Defeat is not treated as proof that faith has failed. Rather, hardship tests and distinguishes people, while final judgment belongs to Allah.

In its closing movement, the surah points to signs in creation and portrays people who remember Allah and reflect on the heavens and earth. Their reflection leads to prayer for forgiveness, protection, and a good end. Allah’s answer promises that no sincere work is lost, whether done by a man or a woman. The surah ends by urging believers to endure, persevere, remain steadfast, and be mindful of Allah.

### The surah’s central message

The material presents the oneness of Allah as the central point shared by the prophets. It describes a line of messengers, from Adam, Nūḥ (Noah), Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), Isḥāq (Isaac), Yaʿqūb (Jacob), Mūsā (Moses), Hārūn (Aaron), and ʿĪsā to Muhammad ﷺ, all calling people to the same truth. The material reports that 124,000 prophets came in different times and places. Their agreement is presented as evidence for the message they carried, while the Qur’an is described as the criterion that distinguishes truth from falsehood. The surah’s practical call follows from this belief: hold firmly to Allah, act with integrity, and meet trial with patience and trust.

### In short

- Āl ʿImrān follows Al-Baqarah by carrying the request for guidance into the challenge of living and defending faith.
- Its central belief is the oneness of Allah and the shared call of the prophets.
- It addresses revelation, the family of Imran, ʿĪsā, relations with other communities, and the trials at Uhud.
- It closes by joining reflection, prayer, perseverance, and mindfulness of Allah.

1.text:
The surah opens with the three separate letters, “Alif-Lãm-Mĩm.” Their meaning is not settled in the explanations gathered here. One view leaves their full meaning with Allah. Another understands them as a challenge: the Qur’an is made from letters familiar to its hearers, yet they cannot produce a book like it. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās connects the letters with the coming account of the Najran delegation. Another interpretation hears them as an oath affirming that Allah is One, with no child or partner.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm”** is not expanded into an agreed ordinary sentence. Some say Allah knows best what He means by these letters. Another explanation says they point to the limits of human power: the Qur’an uses the same letters that form ordinary speech, but people cannot match it. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās links them to the account of the delegation from Najran. It is also said that the letters form an oath declaring Allah’s oneness and denying that He has offspring or a partner.

### What can the letters mean?

The explanations preserve several readings rather than forcing one. The letters may be among the Qur’an’s hidden expressions, whose full meaning is known to Allah. They may also challenge those who hear the Qur’an to produce something like it from the very letters they use themselves. A further reported interpretation treats them as an oath by which Allah declares His unity and freedom from offspring or partnership. The report from Ibn ʿAbbās associates them with the story of the Najran delegation, which the surah returns to later (3:61).

### An inward reading of the letters

An allusive interpretation gives each letter a spiritual association. Alif points to Allah’s sufficiency for a person in every state, even before that person recognizes a need or asks for help. Lām points to His subtle kindness, which may work beyond a person’s awareness. Mīm points to harmony between what Allah decrees and what His close servants seek. This reading connects Mīm with the statement that Allah is upon a matter each day (55:29), understood here as the unfolding of what those close to Him seek. The same interpretation says the letters can loosen the heart’s attachment to ideas formed by necessity (ḍarūra), the senses, and independent reasoning (ijtihād). This reading also treats the unfamiliar letters as a means of loosening the heart’s attachment to ordinary concepts, sensory impressions, and independent reasoning. When the heart is emptied of these, it can turn wholly toward Allah. This is an inward reflection, not a claim that the letters have one agreed lexical translation.

### In short

- The verse names three letters without giving one agreed explanation of their full meaning.
- They have been read as hidden knowledge, a challenge to imitate the Qur’an, an oath of Allah’s oneness, or a reference to the Najran account.
- An inward reading associates the letters with Allah’s sufficiency, subtle kindness, and the heart’s surrender to His decree.

2.text:
The verse declares that “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining.” Allah alone deserves worship. He is perfectly living and does not die or fade, while everything else depends on Him for existence and support. This dependence is offered as a reason that created things, however revered, cannot be gods: what needs another to exist cannot have the independent power that worship requires.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Allah!”** names the One who is the subject of the declaration. The sentence does not present several possible objects of worship. It identifies Allah as the One to whom worship belongs.

**“There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him”** states the oneness of Allah. Worship involves complete humility and submission, so its object must possess the highest power and perfection. Created things cannot sustain their own existence. This applies to idols made of stone or water, to trees, and even to angels and messengers. They depend on their Creator and therefore are not worthy of worship. Allah alone is independent and deserves it.

**“the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining”** translates the names al-Ḥayy and al-Qayyūm, also rendered together as Al-Hayyul-Qayyum. They describe why He alone has this right. The Ever-Living does not die or pass away. The All-Sustaining exists without beginning and maintains all that exists, while creation always needs Him. The pairing is also understood as saying that Allah is never distracted from a person’s state and never inattentive to it. Whether a person is alone or among others, Allah watches over the inward state.

### Why dependence rules out other gods

The reasoning begins with what worship means. A worshipper submits to the one regarded as supreme in honor and power. Anything that cannot bring itself into existence or keep itself alive has no independent claim to that position. The world and all its inhabitants are sustained by Allah. Their dependence points away from worship of created things and toward the One who lives eternally and sustains them all.

### A report about Allah’s greatest name

A hadith discussed in connection with the opening verses says that Allah’s greatest name is found in these verses. It is mentioned alongside the verse of the Throne, Ayat al-Kursi (2:255), where Allah is also described as Ever-Living and Sustainer. The central point here remains the declaration that Allah alone is worthy of worship.

### In short

- Allah alone deserves worship because He is the Ever-Living and the One who sustains everything.
- Every created thing depends on Him, so no created being can share His right to worship.
- Allah’s watchfulness extends to a person’s inward state in solitude and in company.

3.text:
The verse says that Allah revealed the Book to the Prophet ﷺ “in truth, confirming what came before it,” and also revealed the Torah and the Gospel. The Qur’an is presented as revelation from Allah, not a human invention. Its message of Allah’s oneness continues the guidance brought by earlier prophets. Its agreement with earlier revelation is a further sign that the call is one, even though the books were sent at different times.

### Phrase by phrase

**“He has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book in truth”** means that Allah sent the Qur’an to Muhammad ﷺ. It came with truth and has no doubt in its origin. The revelation is described as coming with Allah’s knowledge, with angels bearing witness to it. One explanation says Gabriel brought the Book to the Prophet ﷺ.

**“confirming what came before it”** means that the Qur’an affirms the earlier revealed books and the truth they carried. Those books also bear witness to the Qur’an, including the glad news of Muhammad’s prophethood. Another explanation stresses that the Qur’an’s doctrine of oneness is not a new claim that contradicts previous prophets. The earlier message and the Qur’an agree in their call to Allah.

**“as He revealed the Torah and the Gospel”** points to the books sent to Mūsā (Moses) and ʿĪsā (Jesus). They were revealed before the Qur’an. The names here refer to the original books revealed to those prophets, not to later books bearing similar names.

### What does confirmation mean?

The Qur’an’s confirmation is not merely that earlier scriptures existed. It affirms the truth in the revelation given before it, including the prophets’ shared call to worship Allah alone. The Qur’an also serves as a witness to that earlier truth. One inward reading describes the Qur’an as fulfilling the promise of Muhammad ﷺ found in earlier books. It pictures his remembrance as present within those revelations and treats his mission as completing the line of prophetic guidance.

### In short

- The Qur’an is described as true revelation from Allah, delivered to Muhammad ﷺ.
- It confirms the truth of earlier revelation and shares the prophets’ call to Allah’s oneness.
- The Torah and Gospel were revealed before the Qur’an to Mūsā and ʿĪsā, while the Qur’an came in stages.

4.text:
The verse completes the account of earlier revelation and describes the Qur’an as a criterion that distinguishes truth from falsehood. It also warns those who reject Allah’s revelations of severe punishment. The closing names Allah as Almighty, whose power cannot be resisted, and as able to carry out retribution. Revelation is therefore both guidance and a standard by which claims and actions are judged.

### Phrase by phrase

**“previously, as a guide for people”** continues the description of the Torah and Gospel: they came before the Qur’an and guided people in their time. One explanation specifies that they guided the Children of Israel away from error. Another treats the revealed books together as guidance toward what is good in this life and the next. A grammatical explanation notes that the word for the Qur’an’s revelation suggests repeated sending, while the wording for the Torah and Gospel points to their being sent in one event.

**“and ˹also˺ revealed the Standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺”** names the criterion. Some explanations understand it broadly as the revealed scriptures that distinguish truth from falsehood. Others identify it with the Qur’an, which clarifies what is lawful and unlawful and separates guidance from error. Its clear signs and explanations make the distinction plain.

**“Surely those who reject Allah’s revelations will suffer a severe torment”** warns those who deny and unjustly refuse the revelations. One explanation places the punishment on the Day of Resurrection. Another says it comes in this world and the next, and specifically connects the warning in this setting with the delegation from Najran.

**“For Allah is Almighty, capable of punishment”** names Him as al-ʿAzīz, the invincible One, and as Lord of retribution. No one can overpower Him or prevent His promise and warning from being carried out. His power is complete, and His punishment for those who reject His signs and oppose His messengers is severe.

### How is the criterion understood?

The explanations differ in how widely they apply the word “Standard.” It can refer to all revealed scripture, since revelation distinguishes truth from falsehood. It can also refer specifically to the Qur’an’s clarification of what is right, including lawful and unlawful conduct. Both readings make the same point: people need Allah’s guidance to judge rightly, and rejecting it has consequences.

### In short

- Earlier scriptures guided their people before the Qur’an was revealed.
- The “Standard” is understood as revealed scripture generally or the Qur’an’s clear distinction between right and wrong.
- Those who reject revelation face severe punishment, and Allah has the power to carry out His warning.

5.text:
The verse states, “Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah.” It presents Allah’s knowledge as complete, reaching every existent thing and every detail. The heavens and earth are named as the widest domains people can perceive, not as limits on what He knows. This knowledge also means that no breath, need, or hardship is outside His awareness.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens”** includes every existent thing in both realms. Allah knows universals and particulars, and no particle exists there without Him as its originator and creator. A person does not draw a single breath without it being known to Him.

**“is hidden from Allah”** means His knowledge misses nothing. He governs every quality and attribute. One inward explanation distinguishes ʿumūm, the generality of people, from khuṣūṣ, the spiritual elect. Every person’s need is known, and Allah fulfills a need and suffices in calamity. The point is not that some things are concealed from Him, but that His knowledge and care reach every state.

### In short

- Allah knows every existent thing in the heavens and earth, from the largest to the smallest.
- No breath or personal need is hidden from Him.
- An inward reading adds that He meets needs and suffices through hardship.

6.text:
Allah is the One who “shapes you in the wombs of your mothers as He wills.” The verse joins His creative power to His sole right to be worshipped: He forms each person, and He alone is Almighty and All-Wise. The explanations describe many forms and conditions, including male and female, different appearances, and different destinies. The verse also answers claims that ʿĪsā (Jesus) is divine: he was formed in his mother’s womb, like other human beings, by Allah’s will.

### Phrase by phrase

**“He is the One Who shapes you in the wombs of your mothers as He wills”** means that Allah creates and gives form before birth. He makes people male or female, tall or short, handsome or otherwise, and gives them differing conditions. One explanation also mentions differing complexions and whether a person will be happy or miserable. The variety of human beings, including their distinct features, is presented as a sign of His power and wisdom.

**“There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him”** follows from the fact that He alone creates. ʿĪsā was formed in a womb and developed through stages, as other people do. The verse cited in this connection describes creation in the womb through successive stages and three veils of darkness (39:6). A created servant cannot be the Creator.

**“the Almighty, All-Wise”** means that Allah’s power cannot be overcome and that His acts and decisions have wisdom. He chooses the forms and conditions of those He creates.

### What do the reports about Allah’s form mean?

The discussion includes reports using the language of Allah’s form. In a sound report, Muṣṭafā (Muhammad ﷺ) is quoted as saying that Allah created Adam in His form and that Adam’s height was sixty cubits. Another version says “in the form of His face.” The explanations preserve a disagreement over how to understand such reports. Some interpreters turn the pronoun away from Allah and interpret the wording. Others, identified as the people of the Sunnah, accept the outward wording without asking how it applies. They insist that Allah has no equal and that imagining likeness between Him and creation is an error.

Other reports are cited without a grading here. Ibn ʿAbbās is said to have reported that the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord in the most beautiful form. Abū Umāma al-Bāhilī relates a longer account in which the Prophet ﷺ is addressed and asked what the Higher Plenum are disputing. Jābir ibn Samura and Anas are also named in reports describing the Lord appearing in the most beautiful form. Anas further reports that Allah will remind Adam of the form He bestowed on him. The longer account is said to be discussed elsewhere.

A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās also tells of Mūsā speaking angrily to the Children of Israel and calling them donkeys when they objected to a prohibition. Allah is then said to have asked Mūsā whether he would liken creatures He created in His form to donkeys. The material also says that reports about the Resurrection describe Allah coming to people in a form other than the one by which they recognize Him. These reports are presented alongside the warning not to imagine that Allah resembles His creation.

### In short

- Allah gives each person form in the womb and does so with power and wisdom.
- Because Allah creates, He alone deserves worship. The formation of ʿĪsā in a womb is given as evidence that he is created, not divine.
- Reports about Allah’s form are interpreted differently, while the explanations that accept their outward wording warn against imagining any likeness to creation.
- Several reports describe the Prophet ﷺ seeing Allah in a beautiful form, and the material distinguishes a sound report from other reports whose grading it does not state.

7.text:
The verse begins, “He is the One Who has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book,” then describes its clear and elusive passages. Coming after the affirmation of Allah’s oneness, it answers doubts about revelation and gives readers both a way to approach it and a warning about what can go wrong. Clear verses form the foundation. Passages whose full meaning is uncertain should be read in light of those foundations, not used to force a preferred claim. Those grounded in knowledge accept the whole Book as coming from Allah, while people who chase ambiguity to create doubt risk leading themselves and others astray.

### Phrase by phrase

**“He is the One Who has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book”** introduces the Qur’an as revelation from Allah to Muhammad ﷺ, brought by Gabriel. It is the shared origin of the clear verses and the verses whose meaning is not immediately apparent. Its parts are not in conflict with one another.

**“of which some verses are precise”** describes the muhkam verses, those whose meaning is established and clear. **“they are the foundation of the Book”** explains their role. They are Umm al-Kitab, the Mother of the Book, because they provide the basic principles to which other passages are referred. They include teachings that are clear enough to be acted on: obligations, limits, what is allowed and prohibited, and rules that are to be believed and followed. One explanation calls these the majority of the Qur’an and the reference point when a passage is disputed. Another says their clear meanings can be understood by a reader who knows the rules of Arabic grammar. 

The clear verses are also described as containing proof of Allah, protection for His servants, and answers to false claims. Muḥammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar describes them as proof of the Lord, protection for servants, and a rebuttal of opponents. Their meaning is not to be distorted. One explanation gives the command to recite what Allah has made binding (6:151) as an example. The Qur’an can be called clear in the sense that it has no imperfection, and its parts can also be described as resembling one another in beauty and truthfulness. This is why readers are asked to reflect on it as a whole: a revelation from Allah would not contain contradictions (4:82).

**“while others are elusive”** refers to the mutashabih verses, whose meaning is not clear to everyone and may appear to allow more than one interpretation. Some explanations include passages that describe unseen matters, such as Allah’s attributes and the realities of the next life, which cannot be fully grasped through ordinary language in this world. For example, “a human hand” can be understood directly, while “Allah’s hand” is an allegorical expression whose full reality exceeds human perception. Another classifies among them abrogated passages, parables, oaths, and matters to be believed in but not directly put into practice. Some say the opening letter combinations of surahs are examples. A separate explanation describes the people well-grounded in knowledge as those with a sound understanding of the Torah, naming ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions. A reading of those letters by numerical values, called al-Jumal, is also mentioned as something some people have pursued.

**“Those with deviant hearts follow the elusive verses seeking ˹to spread˺ doubt through their ˹false˺ interpretations”** describes people who leave the clear foundations and build arguments from passages with several possible readings. They seek Al-Fitnah, meaning confusion and division, and try to make the unclear wording support their own claims. One explanation says that such arguments can be used to mislead followers and make an innovation look as if it were proved by the Qur’an. The verse therefore warns against turning an uncertain phrase into a weapon against a clear teaching.

The example given is the claim that ʿĪsā (Jesus) is divine because he is described as Allah’s spirit and word given to Mary. That claim sets those expressions against clear verses identifying ʿĪsā as a servant blessed by Allah (43:59) and comparing his creation with Adam’s (3:59). Those clear passages establish that ʿĪsā is created and a messenger, not divine. The same method applies elsewhere: an interpretation of an unclear verse must not contradict a clear one.

**“but none grasps their ˹full˺ meaning except Allah”** raises a question about where to pause in the reading. Some understand the verse to mean that Allah alone knows the true reality of the elusive passages. Others connect the next words to this phrase and hold that people firmly grounded in knowledge can understand their explanation, though not the unseen reality behind them. Both readings distinguish what people can explain from what remains known only to Allah.

The word ta’wil can mean either the true reality to which something ultimately leads or its explanation. If it means the ultimate reality, only Allah knows it. For example, the full reality of the promised Resurrection is beyond present experience (7:53). If it means explanation, scholars can understand some of what is meant. The word is used for explaining a dream (12:36), and for the later realization of a dream (12:100). A statement about Allah coming with the angels in rows (89:22) is also explained in a straightforward way as describing what will happen. These different senses help explain why scholars differ over the stopping point in the verse.

One report from Ibn ʿAbbās divides explanation into four kinds: what Arabs know through their language, what no one may claim ignorance of, what scholars know, and what only Allah knows. Ibn ʿAbbās also said he was among those grounded in knowledge who knew the explanation. The Prophet ﷺ prayed that he be given knowledge of the religion and taught the interpretation. These reports are consistent with the view that some meanings can be understood while ultimate realities remain beyond human reach.

**“As for those well-grounded in knowledge, they say”** introduces their response. **“We believe in this ˹Quran˺”** and **“it is all from our Lord”** express their humility and trust. Those grounded in knowledge accept both the clear and the elusive verses as true and do not force the latter to contradict the former. They follow interpretations transmitted through the Companions and early generations, and hold the Qur’an and Sunnah together. They may explain what can be understood, but acknowledge the limits of their knowledge. They do not boast about what they know or belittle others. Ibn al-Mundhir records Nafiʿ ibn Yazid describing them as humble before Allah, seeking His pleasure and not exaggerating about those above them or looking down on those below them.

**“But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason”** means that reflection and sound understanding are needed to keep the whole Book in view. A person must not isolate an uncertain phrase from the clear teachings that explain it.

### What are the clear and elusive verses?

The clear verses are the foundation for belief and practice. They include established rulings and teachings that can be understood and acted upon. The elusive verses are those whose definite meaning is not apparent, whether because they concern realities beyond present human experience or because their wording can carry several readings. Explanations differ over whether abrogated rulings, parables, oaths, and the opening letters belong in this category. The practical rule offered across these explanations is consistent: read the less clear in light of the clear, and do not use an uncertain reading to overturn an established teaching.

There is also a distinction between the Qur’an being clear as a whole and containing passages that are elusive to some readers. The whole Book is described as free of defect and internally consistent. Its parts resemble one another in truth and beauty. That does not mean every reader can immediately determine the full meaning of every passage.

### Why do people pursue ambiguity?

The verse criticizes not careful study but a heart set on distortion. People who seek confusion take an expression with several possible meanings and choose the one that serves their agenda. The example of ʿĪsā shows why this is dangerous. A reader cannot isolate descriptions such as “spirit” or “word” while ignoring the clear statements that identify him as a created servant. Clear verses govern interpretation. They are not discarded whenever an ambiguous phrase seems to offer a desired conclusion.

The material gives historical examples of people who pursued hidden or numerical readings. Some Jewish opponents, including Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Ḥuyayy ibn Akhtab, and Judayy ibn Akhtab, are said to have treated the opening letters as numbers through al-Jumal and tried to predict how long the community would last. Another explanation names particular people who sought discord by fixing a future meaning to the letters. These accounts are presented as examples of the very danger the verse names: turning what is uncertain into a claim that serves one’s own purpose.

### Where should the reader pause?

The verse can be read with a pause after “except Allah.” On that reading, only Allah knows the full reality of the elusive verses, and those grounded in knowledge continue by saying they believe in all of them. Another reading joins “those well-grounded in knowledge” to the preceding phrase. They know the explainable meanings, while accepting that the final reality belongs to Allah. Both readings are reported, and the distinction in ta’wil helps explain them. If ta’wil means the final reality, the pause after Allah is fitting. If it means explanation, knowledgeable people may share in understanding it. A pause at this point is reported from ʿĀʾishah, ʿUrwah, Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, and Abū Nahik. Others pause after the words about those firmly grounded in knowledge, taking them as part of the statement about who understands the explanation.

A hadith reported from ʿĀʾishah warns against following the unclear passages to sow discord. The Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and said that when people are seen pursuing its ambiguous parts, they are the people Allah has described, so believers should beware of them. Aḥmad recorded the report, and similar wording is recorded by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and Abū Dāwūd.

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī reported another warning from the Prophet ﷺ about three dangers for his ummah, the community of believers. One is that people become wealthy, envy one another, and fall into division and bloodshed. Another is that people treat the Book carelessly, as unqualified readers claim complete understanding from translations and make the verses whose meaning is not meant to be fully grasped the focus of argument. The third is that people stop increasing their knowledge after gaining some. The report is attributed to al-Ṭabarānī. It warns both against overconfidence and against allowing learning to stagnate.

### What does an inward reading add?

An allusive reading begins with the word “He.” It treats this not as a name or an attribute but as a pointer to Allah’s being, beyond location and beyond the limits of created attributes. It also reflects on the pronoun’s two letters, h and w: they begin in the throat at different points, suggesting that all things begin through Allah’s power and return by His decree.

A story is told of Shurayḥ ʿĀbid seeing a dervish in the sanctuary calling on Allah as “He, other than whom there is no he.” A voice from the unseen tells him that the reward for his first utterance will be recorded until the Resurrection. Another story tells of a person asked his name, origin, and wish, who answered “He” each time. When the name Allah was spoken, he was overcome and died. These stories express the inward reading’s focus on turning wholly toward Allah. A poetic reflection says that people may picture the divine name in a hundred ways, yet loving remembrance leaves them aware of their inability to describe Him fully.

This reading also distinguishes the clear and difficult passages as the outward law, or shariah, and the inward reality, or haqiqah. The clear guides ordinary people toward blessing through understanding and practice. The difficult points toward realities that cannot be fully grasped. This allusive reflection does not cancel the practical rule given above: the clear foundation remains the guide for reading what is less clear.

### In short

- The clear verses are the foundation for belief and practice. Less clear passages must be understood in their light.
- People go astray when they use ambiguity to create division or to force a preferred claim, as in arguments about ʿĪsā.
- Scholars differ over whether only Allah knows the ta’wil or whether knowledgeable people can explain some of it. The full reality remains with Allah.
- The Prophet ﷺ warned against chasing ambiguous passages to cause discord and against neglecting sound, continuing knowledge.
- The people of understanding affirm the whole Qur’an, remain humble about its limits, and ask Allah for steadfast guidance.

8.text:
Those grounded in knowledge answer the warnings of the previous verse with a prayer: “Our Lord! Do not let our hearts deviate after you have guided us.” They know that understanding and faith are gifts that can be lost, so they ask Allah to keep them firm and grant them mercy. The prayer does not claim that a person’s learning or good deeds make steadfastness an entitlement. It asks the Giver for help.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Our Lord! Do not let our hearts deviate after you have guided us”** asks Allah to keep the heart from turning away from truth after being shown the right path. The prayer follows the warning about people who pursue unclear verses to support false readings. The worshippers ask not to become like them. One explanation says guidance and deviation are in Allah’s power: He inclines a heart toward good or allows it to turn away. For that reason, people concerned about faith ask Him for firmness rather than relying on themselves.

The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have prayed, “O Turner of hearts, make our hearts firm upon the faith You have chosen.” Umm Salamah reported that he used to make this supplication, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr recorded it. The prayer asks that Allah not allow confusion or straying to take hold, but keep the heart steady in service and in the Sunnah.

**“Grant us Your mercy”** asks for more than a reward earned by deeds. The prayer seeks the mercy that strengthens the heart, increases faith and certainty, and protects it from misguidance. An inward explanation stresses that mercy is Allah’s generosity, not payment for acts of obedience. Human actions are not a claim on Allah. The servant asks Him to overlook shortcomings and give from His bounty.

**“You are indeed the Giver ˹of all bounties˺”** recognizes Allah as the One who gives guidance, mercy, and firmness. Another explanation reads the title as the One who gave prophethood and Islam to Muhammad ﷺ. The prayer therefore looks to Allah as the giver of both the message and the ability to remain faithful to it.

### What does the prayer teach about steadfastness?

The prayer follows the account of two kinds of readers: those who stay with the clear foundations and those whose hearts turn toward confusion. Even a person grounded in knowledge needs Allah’s help. The Prophet ﷺ himself often asked for firmness. The prayer also gives a way to meet uncertainty: acknowledge human limits, avoid arguments that lead away from guidance, and ask Allah for mercy and steadiness.

An inward reading describes supplication as reaching its aim when the heart is clear, the present moment is given to remembrance, and the tongue is sincere. Its deeper request is for a life of service shaped by the Sunnah. Mercy is sought as a gift, not as a wage. A spiritual teacher from a Tariqah, a path of spiritual discipline, reflected on the verse about deeds becoming scattered dust (25:23) and found comfort in the thought that a person may be freed from relying on inadequate actions and attach the heart instead to Allah’s mercy.

### In short

- The people of knowledge ask Allah to keep their hearts steady after guidance.
- They seek mercy that strengthens faith, not a payment earned by their deeds.
- The Prophet ﷺ also prayed for firmness, and the verse teaches believers to depend on Allah for it.

9.text:
The prayer continues with confidence in the promised gathering: “Our Lord! You will certainly gather all humanity”. Allah will bring people together for judgment and will not fail to keep His promise. The believers ask for steadfastness because they are concerned with the final account, not only with the ease or success of this life.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Our Lord! You will certainly gather all humanity”** affirms that all people will be brought back after death. They will stand before Allah, who will judge between them and settle what they disputed. The reckoning, the crossing over the Bridge, the Scale, Paradise, and Hell are also named among the realities of that promised Day. Their deeds will be answered with reward or punishment.

**“for the ˹promised˺ Day”** identifies the Day of Resurrection. **“about which there is no doubt”** states that it is certain, not a possibility or a figure of speech. One inward reading distinguishes two gatherings. In this life, the hearts of those who love Allah gather in nearness and remembrance. In the next, all people gather for reward and punishment and face its terrors.

**“Surely Allah does not break His promise”** means that the promised return, judgment, and recompense will take place. The prayer’s mention of the promise shows why the worshippers ask to remain guided: they seek to meet that Day on the right path.

### In short

- All humanity will be gathered after death for judgment.
- The Day is certain, and Allah will fulfill His promise of return and recompense.
- The prayer for guidance is made with the final meeting with Allah in view.

10.text:
The verse warns that “neither the wealth nor children of the disbelievers will be of any benefit to them against Allah.” Possessions and family cannot protect a person from judgment or punishment. The verse says the disbelievers will be fuel for the Fire. These verses prepare for the coming declaration that the opponents will be overcome. The warning is not an argument against having wealth or children. An inward reading says possessions can help a believer when used rightly, but they become a danger when a person exceeds what is needed and lets them lead to rebellion.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Indeed, neither the wealth nor children”** names two forms of worldly security people may rely on. Abundance in property or descendants cannot shield a person from Allah’s judgment. Other passages warn that wealth and children can be part of a test in this life (9:55), and that a brief period of worldly prosperity should not deceive the disbeliever (3:196, 3:197).

**“of the disbelievers will be of any benefit to them against Allah”** means these things cannot save those who reject Allah, His messengers, and His revelation from punishment. The warning is also expressed by saying that excuses will not help the wrongdoer on the Day when the curse and evil home are his (40:52). Another passage calls those worshipped besides Allah, together with their worshippers, fuel for Hell (21:98).

Some explanations identify the disbelievers in the immediate setting with Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions. Another identifies them as Abū Jahl and his companions. The verse’s warning is broader than either identification: wealth and children do not avail those who disbelieve.

**“and they will be the fuel for the Fire”** means that they themselves become what feeds the Fire. A grammatical note distinguishes the word for fuel from a similar word for the act of burning. Their possessions and children do not rescue them from this end.

### Can worldly possessions serve a good purpose?

An inward explanation distinguishes the disbeliever’s reliance on possessions from the believer’s responsible use of them. Wealth can help a believer when its obligations are met and it is used to seek the lasting good of the next life. Muṣṭafā (Muhammad ﷺ) is reported to have praised wholesome possessions in the hands of a wholesome person and described them as a help toward mindfulness of Allah. The Qur’an’s instruction to use what Allah has given to seek the next life is cited in this connection (28:77).

The same reading traces how material provision can support worship and tawhid, the oneness of Allah: food, drink, and clothing sustain the body. The body can then perform acts of obedience, and those acts can serve the heart’s recognition of Allah, the Lord of the Worlds. But wealth should remain within the measure of sufficiency. When people exceed that measure and become self-satisfied, possessions can lead to rebellion, as the Qur’an warns (96:6-7). The Prophet ﷺ prayed that his family’s food be kept at a sufficient level. A lawful estate belonging to Abu'l-Qāsim Kurragānī is given as an example of having enough without making abundance the goal.

Thus, the verse does not make possessions inherently evil. It warns that neither wealth nor family can substitute for faith or protect a person from judgment. Used with gratitude and restraint, material provision can support a life directed toward Allah. Treated as an ultimate source of security, it fails and may become a cause of disobedience.

### In short

- Wealth and children cannot protect disbelievers from Allah’s judgment.
- The verse describes those who reject faith as fuel for the Fire.
- Possessions can support a believer’s worship when used responsibly and kept within sufficiency, but they cannot replace faith or become a guarantee of safety.

11.text:
The verse compares the fate of the disbelievers with “the people of Pharaoh and those before them.” They rejected Allah’s signs, so He seized them for their sins. Their history is a warning that rejecting messengers and revelation has consequences, and that no one can escape Allah’s power.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Their fate will be like that of the people of Pharaoh and those before them”** compares the current opponents with earlier communities who rejected the messengers sent to them. One explanation takes the phrase to mean their conduct and practice resembled Pharaoh’s people. Ad-Dahhak, reporting Ibn ʿAbbās, explains it this way. Another reads it as the same outcome and fate. The people of ʿĀd and Thamūd are named among the earlier communities that denied Allah’s signs.

One interpretation connects the warning to the conflict at Badr. It says that the people opposing the Prophet ﷺ had lied about and abused him as Pharaoh’s people had done to Mūsā (Moses), and that their defeat at Badr would resemble the destruction of Pharaoh’s people by drowning. This is presented as a specific application of the comparison, alongside its broader warning about every community that rejects revelation.

**“they all rejected Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins”** explains why those communities were destroyed. They denied the scripture and messenger sent to them. Another explanation stresses that Allah seized them because they persisted in denial and insolence. Their wealth and children could not protect them, as the preceding verse said.

**“And Allah is severe in punishment”** means His punishment is painful and cannot be escaped. Nothing is outside His knowledge or grasp. An inward reading says that insolence became their way, or sunna, and that they did not strive to do good, expressed by the word Ṭamiʿū in the report. They persisted until regret came ʿalayhim, upon them, and the door was closed. Their repentance was then rejected.

### In short

- Pharaoh’s people and earlier communities are examples of the fate of those who reject Allah’s signs.
- One interpretation applies the warning to the opponents at Badr, while the verse also states a general lesson from past communities.
- Allah’s punishment is severe, and no one can escape His knowledge or power.

12.text:
The Prophet ﷺ is told to warn the disbelievers: “Soon you will be overpowered.” The warning speaks of defeat in this life and being gathered for punishment in the next. Its first setting is not every disbeliever in every age. The explanations connect it with the opponents of that time, including the Quraysh and the Jews of Madinah, who challenged the Prophet ﷺ after the victory at Badr.

### Phrase by phrase

**“˹O Prophet!˺ Tell the disbelievers”** is a command to Muhammad ﷺ to deliver the warning openly. One account says that after returning from Badr, he gathered the Jews in the marketplace of Banu Qaynuqaʿ and urged them to accept Islam before the defeat that had come to Quraysh came to them. They replied that the believers had defeated only inexperienced fighters and claimed that the outcome would be different against them.

Another report describes a group of Jews who, after Badr, recognized the Prophet ﷺ as the unlettered messenger foretold to them through Mūsā (Moses). They considered following him but decided to wait for another battle. When the Muslims suffered a setback at Uhud, they became doubtful and said that he was not the promised prophet. They then ended their treaty with him. Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf travelled with sixty riders to meet Abū Sufyān and his companions in Makkah. They agreed to join their efforts against the Prophet ﷺ. The report says this warning was revealed about them.

**“Soon you will be overpowered”** promises defeat in this life. Some explanations specify that those addressed would be killed or taken captive. In the case of the Jews mentioned, the material also describes subjection through the payment of jizya or expulsion. This warning is tied to the opponents of that time, not to every disbeliever without distinction. Another interpretation says that the Meccan idolaters were the direct audience and that Badr was the defeat meant.

**“and driven to Hell—what an evil place to rest!”** points beyond defeat in this world to the gathering in Hell in the Hereafter. The two parts of the warning are distinct: worldly defeat does not replace the final judgment, and the promise of judgment does not make the present consequences unreal.

### What was the setting of the warning?

The explanations give more than one immediate setting. One connects the words to the Jews in Madinah, who challenged Muhammad ﷺ after Badr and were warned after he called them to Islam. Another identifies the disbelievers of Makkah as the ones told that they would be defeated. A report connects the warning to the Jews who first considered believing after Badr, then doubted after Uhud, broke their treaty, and joined Abū Sufyān’s side. These accounts differ in who is directly addressed, but all keep the warning within the conflict of that period rather than applying it indiscriminately to every nonbeliever.

An inward reading says that the disbelievers’ future loss is both separation from Allah in this life and the pain of the Hereafter. Their present faculties may be too weak to recognize the first kind of loss. What seems like a life of ease can therefore hide an inward deprivation, while the punishment of the next life brings that loss into full view.

### In short

- The Prophet ﷺ is told to warn the disbelievers of defeat and the punishment of Hell.
- The warning is connected with the opponents of that time, including the Jews of Madinah and the Quraysh.
- The reports differ on the immediate audience but describe worldly defeat followed by judgment in the Hereafter.

13.text:
The meeting of two armies at Badr is presented as “a sign for you in the two armies that met in battle” showing that Allah supports whom He wills. The believers were far fewer and less equipped than their opponents, yet the encounter ended in their victory. The verse also describes how each side perceived the other’s numbers. The explanations differ over who saw the other as twice as numerous, and one account says their perceptions changed during the battle. The event is a lesson in trusting Allah rather than judging truth by visible strength alone.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Indeed, there was a sign for you in the two armies that met in battle”** points to Badr. The encounter is described as evidence that Allah would make His religion prevail and His messenger victorious. One account says that after Badr the Prophet ﷺ gathered the Jews in Madinah to warn them that they had seen a sign of his prophethood. Another says the event confirmed that the message he carried was true. The later account of Badr is also linked to the promise that a small, patient group can overcome a larger one (8:66).

**“one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial”** identifies the two sides. One was the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, fighting in obedience to Allah. The other was the Quraysh army, including the force associated with Abū Sufyān. The contrast is not simply between two military groups. The verse distinguishes those fighting in faith from those who came in disbelief and, in another account, out of pride and display.

**“The believers saw their enemy twice their number”** has more than one explanation. One reading says the Quraysh thought the Muslims were twice as numerous as they were. This struck fear into them and helped the believers prevail. Another says the Muslims first saw the Quraysh as twice their own number. That sight led them to depend more fully on Allah and ask for His help. A further account says both sides initially saw the opposing force as larger, then each camp appeared smaller to the other when they drew up for battle. This shifting perception encouraged the armies to engage, so that what Allah had decreed would happen.

The explanations give different details of the numbers. One says the Quraysh had about 1,000 men, 700 camels, and 100 horses, while the Muslims had just over 300 men, 70 camels, two horses, six coats of armor, and eight swords. Another gives the Muslim force as 313 and the opposing army as 950. These figures describe a striking difference in manpower and equipment. The report attributed to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd says the Muslims first found the enemy to be twice their number, then looked again and thought there was not one more enemy fighter than their own side. The verse about the meeting says that Allah made each group appear small to the other (8:44). Another verse explains that the meeting occurred so a matter already decreed would be brought about (8:42).

**“But Allah supports with His victory whoever He wills”** explains why the weaker side prevailed. Their victory did not come from their larger resources. Allah strengthened them with His aid. The Qur’an recalls that He had already granted victory at Badr when the believers were few (3:123). Another explanation says that the believers saw their opponents as more numerous and therefore turned to Allah with greater trust. In either reading, Allah’s support, not a force’s visible size, determines the outcome.

**“Surely in this is a lesson for people of insight”** calls readers to think about Allah’s wisdom and decision. An extraordinary victory by a small, poorly equipped group over a much stronger force is not to be explained by worldly advantage. It shows that truth is not unsupported, even when its followers appear weak. People of insight are asked to consider what the event reveals about Allah’s power and the limits of human calculation.

### Why do the accounts differ about what each side saw?

The reports describe the moment from different perspectives. Some say the Quraysh saw the believers as twice their number, which brought fear and despair. Others say the Muslims saw the enemy as twice their number, which deepened their reliance on Allah. A further explanation describes both groups at first seeing the other as larger, then seeing the forces as smaller when the battle lines formed. These accounts do not change the verse’s central point: the appearance of numbers was not the measure of the outcome, and Allah supported whom He willed.

The material also gives different counts for the armies and their equipment. It reports approximately 1,000 Quraysh fighters, 700 camels, and 100 horses, against just over 300 believers, 70 camels, two horses, six coats of armor, and eight swords. Another report gives 313 believers and 950 opponents. The variation is retained rather than collapsed into one exact count.

### What made the encounter a sign?

The sign lay in the imbalance between the two forces and the result. The believers were few and had little equipment. Their opponents had far more men and resources. Yet Allah gave victory to the believers, fulfilling the warning that the disbelievers would be overcome. The account describes this as confirmation of Muhammad’s prophethood and proof that Allah can make His religion prevail. It also provides a worldly example of the final distinction between truth and falsehood.

An inward reading says that physical sight alone does not guarantee insight. When Allah covers a person’s inner sight, sharp eyes do not reveal what matters. When He opens a person’s inward perception, limited outward vision does not prevent understanding. The event therefore asks people not only to look at the numbers but to see what Allah’s support made clear.

### In short

- Badr showed that Allah could grant victory to a small and lightly equipped force.
- Explanations differ over which side saw the other as twice its number and over the exact army counts.
- The event was a sign of Allah’s support, a lesson in trust, and evidence that visible strength does not decide the outcome.

14.text:
After earlier warnings about opposition to Islam and jihad, striving in Allah’s cause, the verse turns to the worldly attractions that can drive people to hostility toward the truth. It lists “the enjoyment of ˹worldly˺ desires—women, children” and other attractions that draw people toward this life. These are not described as evil in themselves. Their appeal is part of the test: will people use them with moderation and remember their return to Allah, or let them take over the heart and make the Hereafter seem unimportant? The verse calls these things temporary enjoyment and points to the better return with Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**“The enjoyment of ˹worldly˺ desires—women, children”** names family among the attractions people love. The explanations say women are mentioned first because desire for them can be a powerful test for men. Marriage can be good when it serves chastity and the raising of children. A report in a Ṣaḥīḥ collection says that the Prophet ﷺ left no temptation more powerful for men than women. Other reports say that the best members of his ummah, the Muslim community, are those with the most wives, and describe a righteous wife as one of the best joys of this life. The Prophet ﷺ is also reported to have said that women and perfume were made beloved to him, while prayer was the comfort of his eye. ʿĀʾishah is reported to have said that nothing was dearer to him than women, except horses, with another version reversing the order.

The desire for children can become a temptation when it is driven by pride or boasting. It is praised when parents hope to raise worshippers who increase the community of Muhammad ﷺ in worshipping Allah alone. A report encourages marrying a loving and fertile spouse so that the Prophet ﷺ may take pride in the size of his community on the Day of Resurrection.

**“treasures of gold and silver, fine horses, cattle, and fertile land”** names material wealth and the means of livelihood. The term qanaṭīr al-muqanṭarah means amassed or heaped-up wealth and points to a large amount. Scholars, including al-Ḍaḥḥāk, differed about the precise measure of a qintar. Abū Hurayrah is reported to have described it as twelve thousand uqiyahs, each of which he considered greater than what lies between the heavens and earth. Ibn Jarīr recorded that report. The point of the different definitions is the abundance represented by the word.

The attraction of wealth can lead to arrogance and the desire to control or dominate others. It can also be used to care for family and relatives, help the poor, and carry out acts of worship. In the latter case, it is praised. The same distinction applies to horses. One person keeps them for service in Allah’s cause and may use them in battle when needed. Another collects them for pride and hostility toward Islam and the Muslim community, which brings blame. A third keeps horses to meet ordinary needs and raise offspring, while paying what is due to Allah. In that case they can be a means of sufficiency. The verse about preparing mounts for defense is cited in this connection (8:60).

Fine, marked horses are explained as branded or beautiful. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid are among those who give this explanation. Others named include as-Suddī, Abū Sinān, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, ʿIkrimah, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abzā is also mentioned. Makhūl says the description can refer to a horse with white markings on its face or feet. A report from Abū Dharr, recorded by Aḥmad, says that an Arabian horse makes two supplications at dawn, asking Allah to make it among the owner’s most valued possessions. “Cattle” includes camels, cows, and sheep. “Fertile land” means cultivated ground used to grow plants.

**“has been made appealing to people”** points to a desire placed in human nature. An explanation says that Allah made lawful goods attractive as a test. Without a desire for food, shelter, family, work, and useful possessions, people might not farm, take a job, trade, build, or earn. Their natural attraction helps sustain human life and society. It can also give people some sense of the blessings of the unseen next life. The test is whether a person becomes absorbed in present enjoyment and forgets the return to Allah, or uses these means while keeping the final account in view.

The same attraction has a further purpose: people are tested over whether they will take the glitter of this life as their final goal or recognize it as temporary. The Holy Qur’an describes the world’s adornments as a test of who acts best (18:7). Where harmful deeds are made attractive, the material also speaks of Satan’s role (8:48, 16:63, 27:24, 29:38). Lawful pleasures are not condemned merely because they are attractive. The danger is crossing the limits set by Allah or letting them displace concern for the life to come.

**“These are the pleasures of this worldly life”** says that the listed things are temporary. Their comfort lasts only for a time, then fades. They can support a person’s life and work, but they are not the lasting destination. One explanation compares worldly possessions to water around a boat. Water beneath the boat helps it travel. If water enters and fills the boat, it sinks. In the same way, possessions can support a person’s role in this world and the next when kept in their proper place. When love of them fills the heart, it can destroy the person’s spiritual life. The saying is attributed to Rūmī.

Another explanation notes that love of these things can keep society moving. Workers earn, employers hire, merchants sell, and customers obtain what they need because people want goods and livelihood. The same desires can be used for good or can become obstacles. A person who enjoys lawful blessings and uses their means to prepare for the Hereafter can benefit in both lives. A person who gives them the heart’s full attention may lose the lasting life and turn those very blessings into punishment.

**“but with Allah is the finest destination”** directs desire toward the lasting return. The best outcome is not the accumulation of worldly goods but the final home with Allah. The verse calls for moderation: people may seek good things and keep what meets genuine needs, but they must not use them unlawfully or become so engrossed that they forget life after death.

### Why are ordinary desires part of a test?

The explanations say these attractions are not pointless. They help people live, support families, and maintain the work of society. They may also awaken a desire for lasting blessings. Their danger lies in mistaking the means for the final goal. A person can use wealth, family, and work to serve Allah and prepare for the Hereafter. Or the person can become so attached to them that friends, family, and social standing matter more than the truth.

A person who treats worldly means as a path can enjoy what is lawful without losing sight of the lasting return. Another person may spend wealth and attention on worldly security until the next life no longer enters the plan. A verse warns that wealth and children can become a punishment in this life (9:55). The central distinction is moderation and purpose, not a rejection of every worldly blessing.

### What does the inward reading of the test add?

An allusive reading, in a report from Muṣṭafā (the Prophet ﷺ), the leader of the children of Adam, portrays Paradise as a destination reached through hardship. After Allah created Paradise, He sent Gabriel to see it. Gabriel said that whoever heard of its blessings would aim to enter it. Allah then surrounded the road to Paradise with hardship, disappointment, and desires that cannot all be fulfilled. The traveler must cross that trial to reach the destination. Shaykh al-Islām Anṣārī reflected that suffering can conceal happiness and that disappointment may lie above a thousand treasures. He asks how he could have known that the way to companionship with Allah passes through bewilderment and difficulty. Another image calls the Kaaba a resting place for Allah’s friends, with a vast desert and many stations to cross before reaching it. The seeker must keep travelling through the desert of love to reach Allah’s acceptance. The imagery presents difficulty as part of the test, not as proof that the destination is absent.

### In short

- Family, wealth, horses, livestock, and farmland are attractive parts of worldly life, but they are also a test.
- These blessings may be used for worship and care of others, or they may lead to pride, excess, and neglect of the Hereafter.
- The world’s comfort is temporary. The best return is with Allah, so the believer keeps worldly means within proper limits.
- The inward reading presents hardship as part of the road to lasting reward.

15.text:
The Prophet ﷺ is told to ask, “Shall I inform you of what is better than ˹all of˺ this?” The answer contrasts the temporary attractions of verse 14 with lasting blessings for those mindful of Allah: Gardens, purified spouses, and Allah’s pleasure. The greatest promise is not simply a place of comfort. It is Allah’s approval, with no fear that it will be withdrawn.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Shall I inform you of what is better than ˹all of˺ this?’”** directs Muhammad ﷺ to call people away from being absorbed in perishable pleasures by telling them about what lasts. The question is meant as an invitation and assurance, not a request for information.

**“Those mindful ˹of Allah˺ will have Gardens with their Lord”** promises Paradise to those who keep away from disbelief, idolatry, indecency, and what Allah has forbidden, and who obey Him. Taqwa, being mindful of Allah, is shown through obedience and restraint. The material says Gardens have degrees corresponding to degrees of taqwa. It mentions the Garden of Refuge and the Garden of Eden, with Allah’s greatest approval as higher still. An explanation applies the promise to Abū Bakr and the believers with him. A passage about the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains desire is cited (79:40-41). Another promises good dwellings in the Gardens (9:72). The highest goal is Allah’s pleasure.

**“under which rivers flow, to stay there forever”** describes a permanent home rather than a passing pleasure. The rivers are described as carrying water, milk, honey, and wine unlike anything people have known. The people of Paradise do not die or leave. Their blessings do not diminish or disappear.

**“and pure spouses”** means companions free of the impurities and defects associated with worldly life. The word also carries the sense of purity in character and form. The verse mentions spouses but does not list every possible blessing. Other reports say that if a person in Paradise wishes for a child, the process of pregnancy, birth, and growth will occur at once. Another says that someone who wishes to farm will be given what is needed, and ploughing, sowing, ripening, and harvest will all be completed immediately. These reports are attributed to at-Tirmidhī and al-Ṭabarānī respectively.

Gold and silver are not listed as central rewards because there will be no buying, selling, or need to use money. Whatever people need will be provided. Reports still describe some parts of Paradise as built with bricks of gold and silver. Horses, cattle, farmland, and produce are also not needed there in the way they are in this life, because their benefits will already be provided. Sound hadith reports describe fine horses presented to people in Paradise on Fridays for riding to visit friends and relatives.

**“along with Allah’s pleasure”** names the greatest blessing. One report describes Allah asking the people of Paradise whether they are content and need anything. They answer that they have received everything. Allah then gives them His approval and promises never to be displeased with them. With that approval, there is no fear that their blessings will end or be taken away.

A report from the Prophet ﷺ says that worldly life and what it contains are cursed except what is used to seek Allah’s pleasure. Another version excepts remembrance of Allah, what Allah loves, a religious scholar, and a student of religious knowledge. Ibn Mājah and al-Ṭabarānī report it from Abū Hurayrah.

**“And Allah is All-Seeing of ˹His˺ servants”** means that Allah knows His servants’ deeds and conditions and gives them what is fitting. The reward is not hidden from Him, and He sees how people use the attractions of this life.

### Why are only some blessings named?

The previous verse lists six attractions of earthly life. This verse names three corresponding blessings of the next life: Gardens, purified spouses, and Allah’s approval. Children are not listed because people in Paradise will not need heirs or support, and everyone who had children will have them there. Those who had none will not begin with a desire for children, though reports say their wishes can be granted. Gold and silver are not needed for trade in a place where every need is supplied. Other earthly goods are likewise unnecessary because their benefits are already provided. The list therefore points to the lasting nature of Paradise rather than setting a limit on what its people may enjoy.

### What is greater than the Gardens?

The verse identifies Allah’s pleasure as greater than the other blessings. The people of Paradise will have every need met, but the assurance that Allah is pleased with them and will never be displeased is the highest good. An allusive interpretation also distinguishes levels of taqwa and the Gardens that correspond to them. Its greatest degree is the approval of Allah, greater than the Garden of Eden (9:72). Ibrāhīm (Abraham) is quoted as saying that created things are his enemies except the Lord of the Worlds (26:77). The reading calls the seeker to loosen the heart from everything created and turn it wholly toward Allah.

### In short

- Those mindful of Allah are promised lasting Gardens and purified spouses.
- Paradise includes what its people desire, so worldly things such as money and farmland are not needed there as they are here.
- Allah’s approval is the greatest blessing, and it will never be withdrawn.
- Allah sees His servants and knows their deeds and conditions.

16.text:
The verse describes the al-Muttaqin, those mindful of Allah who receive the promise of Paradise, as people who pray, “Our Lord! We have believed, so forgive our sins.” They acknowledge faith in Allah and His Messenger and ask Him to cover their wrongs and protect them from the Fire. Their request rests on Allah’s mercy, not on a claim that their belief or deeds entitle them to a reward.

### Phrase by phrase

**“who pray, ‘Our Lord! We have believed’”** describes people who affirm faith in Allah, His Book, and His Messenger. The word alladhīna, “those who,” can be read as a further description of the people mindful of Allah, or as a continuation describing those who make the prayer. Another explanation says they follow the sacred law brought by the messengers. Their words and actions are joined: they do not treat faith as a claim with no practice behind it.

**“so forgive our sins”** asks Allah to pardon errors and shortcomings, including sins committed before and after Islam. The prayer covers sins committed before Islam and those committed after embracing it. It is made with reliance on Allah’s bounty and mercy. An inward reading says these servants turn wholly to Allah and seek nearness and intimate friendship, especially when they remember severe trials and afflictions. They ask for help and for a pleasing end.

**“and protect us from the torment of the Fire”** asks Allah to keep punishment away. The prayer recognizes that salvation is in His hands and that people need His protection.

### What does their prayer show?

These are the al-Muttaqin, people who fear Allah and hope for Paradise. Their belief does not make them complacent. They ask for forgiveness and protection, especially when they remember severe trials and afflictions. Their prayer turns away from worldly gain and seeks nearness to Allah and a pleasing end. It is a supplication that joins faith with dependence on divine mercy.

### In short

- The people of faith believe in Allah, His Book, and His Messenger, and seek to live by the sacred law.
- They ask forgiveness for past and present sins and depend on Allah’s mercy.
- They seek protection from the Fire and turn to Allah in times of hardship.

17.text:
The verse expands on the character of those who pray in verse 16. They are “patient, sincere, obedient, and charitable,” and they seek forgiveness before dawn. Their faith appears in steady conduct: they persist in obedience, tell the truth, submit to Allah, give from their wealth, and turn to Him when others are asleep.

### Phrase by phrase

**“˹It is they˺ who are patient”** includes patience in acts of obedience, in avoiding what Allah forbids, and when hardship arrives. An inward reading adds patience through trials without complaint until the seeker reaches Allah.

**“sincere, obedient”** describes truthfulness in faith and submission to Allah. Their words agree with their deeds. Their supplication is matched by action. They stay firm on the path Allah set and follow His sacred law rather than abandoning it for worldly approval.

**“and charitable”** means they spend their wealth in obedience to Allah, care for relatives, help those in need, and comfort the poor. An inward reading says generosity extends beyond property to the effort of the body and sincerity of the heart.

**“and who pray for forgiveness before dawn”** describes seeking Allah’s pardon in the late part of the night. It is a time when many people are unaware or enjoying sleep, so turning to Allah then shows attention and devotion. The verse about Yaʿqūb (Jacob) says he would ask forgiveness for his children (12:98). One explanation says he waited until the late night to make that prayer.

The Prophet ﷺ described Allah descending to the lowest heaven in the last third of each night and calling: whoever asks will be given, whoever calls will be answered, and whoever seeks forgiveness will be forgiven. Several Companions reported this hadith. It is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, the Musnad, and Sunan collections. ʿĀʾishah said that the Prophet ﷺ prayed witr in the early, middle, and later parts of the night, then later in his life restricted it to the later part. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar would ask Nāfiʿ whether the late part of the night had begun, then pray and seek forgiveness until dawn. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded this report.

### What do these qualities look like together?

The qualities describe the whole person. Patience governs the heart, truthfulness guides the spirit, obedience shapes the body, and charity directs wealth toward Allah’s path. The heart is filled with dhikr, remembrance of Allah, while the tongue asks forgiveness. The person is patient in hardship, truthful in seeking, constant in service, and generous with what is available. The inward reading describes such a person as not held back by either worldly reward or fear of punishment, but seeking Allah Himself and the “seat of truthfulness” with an all-powerful King (54:55).

### In short

- The righteous persist in obedience, avoid wrongdoing, and remain patient in hardship.
- They are truthful, obedient, and generous with their wealth and effort.
- They seek forgiveness in the quiet hours before dawn, following the example of the prophets and the Prophet ﷺ.

18.text:
The surah’s opening established tawhid, the oneness of Allah. This verse returns to it and declares that “Allah ˹Himself˺ is a Witness that there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him.” The angels and people of knowledge bear witness as well. Their testimony points to Allah’s oneness, while the statement that He maintains creation in justice describes the order of His rule and sacred law. The verse repeats that there is no god except Him and names Him Almighty and All-Wise.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Allah ˹Himself˺ is a Witness”** means that Allah has made His oneness clear through signs and proofs. His existence, attributes, power, and creativity are visible in creation. The testimony, or shahadah, is not an uncertain human claim. Allah is the most truthful and just witness. He also bears witness to the revelation sent to Muhammad ﷺ (4:166).

A report tells of two Jewish scholars who came from Syria to Madinah. The place matched a description in the Torah of where the final prophet would live. They heard of a pious man called a prophet and went to meet Muhammad ﷺ. His appearance reminded them of the descriptions in their scripture. They asked whether he was Muhammad and then Ahmad. He said that both names applied to him. They asked who the greatest witness in Allah’s Book was. This verse was revealed as the answer, and the two men accepted Islam.

**“that there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him”** is the truth to which Allah bears witness. He alone is Lord and God. Every creature belongs to Him, depends on Him, and needs Him. Allah needs nothing from anyone. The verse repeats the declaration later to emphasize it.

**“and so are the angels and people of knowledge”** names two further groups who testify to Allah’s oneness. The angels carry out His commands. People of knowledge include the prophets, believers, and those who know Islam. The term ulū al-ʿilm, “people of knowledge,” can also include anyone who uses sound inquiry and reflection on the universe to recognize Allah’s unity, even if their knowledge was not acquired through formal religious study. Their testimony is a great honor, since it is joined to the testimony of Allah and the angels. Allah does not need their testimony. Its honor is for them.

Aḥmad recorded a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse at ʿArafāt and then said, “My Lord, I too bear witness to this.” Another report says that whoever recites it and then makes this declaration will be admitted to Paradise. The report describes Allah as promising that He will keep His promise.

**“He is the Maintainer of justice”** means that Allah constantly upholds His creation and acts with justice in everything. The universe’s order is presented as a sign of a single planner and of a Lord who places things rightly. If Allah maintains justice in the larger universe, human beings too are accountable to live by justice. The created world itself is in submission to His appointed order, and people are called to submit their lives to His plan.

**“There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Almighty, All-Wise”** repeats the testimony and describes Allah as invincible in His power and wise in His actions, commands, and decisions. He cannot be overcome, and His wisdom governs what He creates and legislates.

### Why are the angels and people of knowledge named as witnesses?

Their testimony confirms the oneness that Allah has already made clear. The angels know Allah’s command and carry it out. The people of knowledge recognize the signs and proclaim the truth. The verse gives particular honor to those who know, while also widening the term to include people whose careful reasoning leads them to recognize Allah. Their witness is not needed to establish Allah’s unity. Rather, Allah gives them the honor of recognizing and affirming it.

### Reports about reciting the verse

A report says that after reciting the verse at ʿArafāt, the Prophet ﷺ added that he too bore witness. Another report from al-Aʿmash says that a person who recites the verse and follows it with that declaration will be admitted to Paradise. A report from Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī says that reciting Ayat al-Kursi (2:255), this verse, and the passage about Allah’s ownership (3:26) brings forgiveness and care for seventy needs, the least of which is forgiveness.

### An inward reading of the witness

An allusive interpretation pictures Allah bearing witness to Himself before any created being existed. There was no Adam, heaven, earth, light, darkness, visible creation, unseen creation, or human understanding. Allah has no beginning and will have no end. Nothing is outside His power, yet His reality cannot be grasped by imagination or human reasoning. He is the First, the Last, the Outward, and the Inward, and His own knowledge encompasses His essence and attributes.

The angels, prophets, and people of knowledge are honored when their testimony is joined to His. This does not mean Allah needs support from created witnesses. The honor comes from Allah’s generosity in enabling them to know Him. No one can fully comprehend His kingdom or the perfection of His divinity. Knowledge of Him is itself a gift. Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills (2:105).

### In short

- Allah, the angels, and people of knowledge bear witness to Allah’s oneness.
- Allah maintains creation with justice and is Almighty and All-Wise.
- Reports describe the verse’s recitation at ʿArafāt and its use in supplication.
- An inward reading says that Allah’s knowledge of Himself is complete and that human knowledge of Him is a gift.

19.text:
