The verse says that “Allah’s only Way is Islam.” Islam means submission to Allah. The explanations discuss both the shared submission taught by every prophet and the final way brought by Muhammad ﷺ. They also explain that disputes among people who received scripture arose after knowledge came to them, driven by envy and rivalry rather than a lack of evidence.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Certainly, Allah’s only Way is Islam”** uses a word that can mean religion or way. At its broadest, Islam is submission to Allah, belief in His oneness, the Last Day and final reckoning, Paradise and Hell, every prophet and messenger from Adam onward, and the commands they brought. In this sense, the followers of Nūḥ (Noah), Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Mūsā (Moses), and ʿĪsā (Jesus) were Muslims when they submitted to Allah and obeyed the messenger sent in their time. The Qur’an says that Allah assigned the same religion to Nūḥ and the prophets who followed him (42:13). Nūḥ said that he had been commanded to be among those who submit (10:72). Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) prayed to be made Muslims (2:128), and the disciples of ʿĪsā said they bore witness that they submitted (3:52). The Torah was revealed to Mūsā, and the Injīl to ʿĪsā.

The word can also refer specifically to the religion and shariah, the sacred law brought by Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ. One explanation distinguishes the enduring shared faith from the particular laws given to different communities. It says that once Muhammad ﷺ was sent as the final prophet, earlier laws were superseded and the way that remains binding is the one taught by the Qur’an and Sunnah. The well-known hadith of Jibrīl explains Islam in this specific sense. The Holy Qur’an says that anyone seeking a way other than Islam will not have it accepted (3:85). Although the explanations begin with two possible meanings, both conclude that people are called to submit to Allah and follow the messenger sent to them. For the community addressed after Muhammad ﷺ, this means following his message.

An inward interpretation describes submission in three stages. The first is a declaration that protects a person’s life and property. The next is true belief, following the Sunnah, and acting faithfully. The highest is surrendering oneself to Allah’s decree without protest or turning away. Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl’s prayer to be made submitters (2:128), Ibrāhīm’s response to the command “Submit” (2:131), and Yūsuf’s (Joseph’s) prayer to die in submission (12:101) are given as examples of this complete surrender.

**“Those who were given the Scripture did not dispute ˹among themselves˺ out of mutual envy until knowledge came to them”** means that their disagreements arose after revelation and evidence had reached them. They did not differ because guidance was absent. Envy, hatred, rivalry, and fear of losing authority led some to oppose even what they knew to be true. One explanation says that some feared losing their influence among the community. Their disputes were therefore acts of transgression against knowledge.

**“Whoever denies Allah’s signs, then surely Allah is swift in reckoning”** warns that rejecting Allah’s revelations brings judgment. Some explanations say the reckoning begins after death, in barzakh, the state between death and resurrection. The full account of deeds will take place on the Day of Judgment, when denial and disputation are exposed. The verse says Allah is swift in reckoning. Nothing about a person’s denial is hidden from Him.

### What does “Islam” mean here?

The word can mean submission to Allah shared by all prophets, or the specific religious law brought by Muhammad ﷺ. The explanations preserve both senses. Earlier communities were Muslims when they followed the revelation sent to their prophet. The religious laws could differ across prophetic eras, and earlier laws were later superseded. In the period after Muhammad ﷺ, the message brought by him is the way to submit to Allah.

One explanation rejects the idea that all religions can be treated as equally valid paths to salvation merely because a person does good deeds. It calls kufr, disbelief in a basic principle of Islam, rebellion against Allah. It argues that submission and obedience to Allah are essential, and that denying a basic principle of Islam cannot be made acceptable by other good actions or outward morality. It cites a verse saying that some people’s deeds will have no weight on the Day of Judgment (18:105). This is presented as a firm claim about the meaning of the verse, not as an account of every disagreement over the word Islam.

### Why did people who had scripture dispute?

The verse says the dispute followed knowledge. The explanations attribute it to envy and rivalry, including fear of losing power and influence. Some people knew what their scripture said about Muhammad ﷺ but resisted accepting his prophethood. Their opposition was not caused by a lack of evidence, but by a refusal to accept its consequences.

### In short

- Islam means submission to Allah, a call shared by all prophets.
- The explanations also use Islam for the final way brought by Muhammad ﷺ, whose message is followed after his coming.
- Those who had scripture disputed after knowledge reached them because of envy, rivalry, and attachment to authority.
- Allah’s reckoning is certain, and rejection of His signs has consequences.

20.text:
The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ what to say if people dispute with him: “I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have my followers.” It then calls the People of the Scripture and the unlettered people to submit as well. If they do and follow the Prophet’s sacred law, they are guided and set on the path. If they turn away, the Prophet’s duty is only to deliver the message. Allah sees every servant and will judge their response.

### Phrase by phrase

**“So if they argue with you ˹O Prophet˺”** refers to disputes about Allah’s oneness and the truth of Islam. The surah has already answered the claims made against it. The Prophet ﷺ is told not to be consumed by arguments that do not change the truth.

**“say, ‘I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have my followers’”** means that the Prophet ﷺ and those who follow him devote their worship to Allah alone and have accepted His guidance. One explanation highlights the word “my face” in the underlying expression, since the face is the most honored part of a person. Once it turns in submission, the rest of the person follows. The followers accept the same faith and way. The Prophet ﷺ also describes his way as a call to Allah, which he and those who follow him carry out with clear knowledge (12:108).

**“And ask those who were given the Scripture and the illiterate ˹people˺, ‘Have you submitted yourselves ˹to Allah˺?’”** extends the call to Jews and Christians, as well as the Arab idolaters who were not given a scripture. The question is an invitation to submit sincerely and follow the message brought by Muhammad ﷺ.

**“If they submit, they will be ˹rightly˺ guided”** means that accepting Allah’s message and following the Prophet ﷺ leads them from error to guidance.

**“But if they turn away, then your duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺”** comforts the Prophet ﷺ. He is responsible for conveying Allah’s guidance, not for forcing people to accept it. Their return and reckoning belong to Allah. One explanation notes that this statement preceded the later command to fight, so the immediate duty described here is to deliver the message.

**“And Allah is All-Seeing of ˹His˺ servants”** means He fully knows who accepts and who rejects, and will judge each person accordingly. His knowledge includes their actions, intentions, and response to the call. His perfect wisdom means that He is not questioned for what He does, while His servants will be questioned (21:23).

### Is the message meant for all people?

The explanations say Muhammad ﷺ was sent to all people, not only to one group. The Qur’an calls him a messenger to all humanity (7:158) and describes him as a warner to all peoples (25:1). Two hadith collections and others report that he sent letters to rulers and communities, including Arabs and non-Arabs, People of the Scripture and those without a scripture.

Muslim records Abū Hurayrah’s report that the Prophet ﷺ warned that anyone from his ummah, Jewish or Christian, who hears his message and dies without faith faces the Fire. The Prophet ﷺ is also reported to have said that he was sent to all peoples, described in one saying as the red and black, and that earlier prophets were sent to their own people while he was sent to all humanity.

### What is the Prophet’s duty when people refuse?

The verse separates the Prophet’s duty from the response of his audience. He conveys the message clearly. Whether people accept or reject it is not his responsibility to control. Allah sees what they do and will decide with full knowledge. An inward reading applies Allah’s taṣrīf, His directing of circumstances, to the difference between people’s states. The caller should continue advising in public and private, while not allowing the varied responses of people to unsettle the heart. The task is to counsel and deliver, while Allah governs the outcome.

### In short

- The Prophet ﷺ and his followers submit to Allah alone and invite others to do the same.
- The call is addressed to the People of the Scripture and to those without a revealed scripture.
- If people refuse, the Prophet’s duty is still to convey the message. Allah sees and judges every servant.
- Muhammad ﷺ is described as a messenger to all humanity.

21.text:
Following the call to submit in the previous verse (3:20), this verse condemns those who deny Allah’s signs, kill prophets unjustly, and kill people who call for justice. It announces “a painful punishment” and leads into the description of wasted deeds and helplessness (3:22). The explanations connect these actions with repeated rejection of revelation and arrogance toward those who called people to truth and fairness.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Indeed, those who deny Allah’s signs”** refers in one explanation to people who reject the message of Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur’an. It also includes those who deny earlier revelation, such as the Injīl. Their rejection is part of a larger refusal to accept messengers and follow what Allah revealed.

**“kill the prophets unjustly”** condemns killing messengers who had committed no crime and were calling people to the truth. Another reading of the verb can mean fighting against the prophets. The verse stresses that they were opposed without right.

A report attributed to the Prophet ﷺ and narrated by Ibn Abī Ḥātim says that the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at one time. One hundred and seventy righteous elders stood up and urged them to uphold justice, and they too were killed that same day. The report illustrates the severity of the rejection described.

**“and kill people who stand up for justice”** refers to those who call others to fairness and just conduct. One explanation describes them as people who encourage moderation in actions and morals. Another says they called people to Allah’s oneness. Killing those who urge justice is presented as an extreme act of arrogance and defiance.

**“give them good news of a painful punishment”** uses the language of good news sarcastically. The punishment is painful and humiliating. The explanations say that rejection of truth and arrogance toward people lead to disgrace in this life and punishment in the Hereafter. An inward reading describes the offenders as having been abandoned to deprivation, or khidhlān, then moved from one state of disgrace to another and finally to punishment.

### Why is punishment called good news?

The phrase is deliberately ironic. These people expected to prevail, yet the message delivered to them is a painful and humiliating outcome. Their deeds and status will not protect them from the consequence of rejecting truth and opposing those who call for justice.

### In short

- The verse condemns denial of revelation, unjust killing of prophets, and killing those who call for justice.
- A report describes forty-three prophets and one hundred and seventy righteous elders being killed on the same day.
- The “good news” of punishment is sarcastic and announces humiliation and pain.

22.text:
The verse says that the people described just before it (3:21) have deeds that “are wasted in this world and the Hereafter,” and that “they will have no helpers.” Good works cannot compensate for rejecting Allah’s signs and committing grave injustice. They will receive no reward for deeds that lacked faith, and no one will protect them from punishment.

### Phrase by phrase

**“They are the ones whose deeds are wasted in this world and the Hereafter”** means their good actions have become invalid and will bring no lasting benefit. The explanations include acts of charity and kindness to relatives among the works that fail when they are not joined to faith. Their denial, killing, and rejection of justice undo the value they expected their deeds to have.

An inward reading says that they have lost Allah’s help in both abodes. Their works do not reach their hopes in this life, and they find no success or realization of their hopes in the next. The rejection of Allah’s power and the failure to bear witness to His oneness leave them without support.

**“And they will have no helpers”** means there will be no protector who can save them from Allah’s punishment. Their position, allies, and good works cannot rescue them.

### In short

- Their deeds bring no reward in this life or the next because they rejected faith and justice.
- No helper or protector can save them from Allah’s punishment.

23.text:
The verse asks, "Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures?" (3:23) They claimed to follow revelation, yet when invited to let Allah’s Book settle a dispute, some turned away. The explanations connect this refusal to Jews who knew that the Torah supported the truth but did not want its judgment when it went against their preferences.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures?"** (3:23) addresses Muhammad ﷺ and points to people who received the Torah, the Injīl (Gospel), and other scripture. The verse challenges those who claim to follow their books while refusing what those books require. One explanation says their scripture contained knowledge that confirmed Muhammad’s prophethood. Another centers the passage on the Torah’s judgment in a legal dispute.

**“Yet when they are invited to the Book of Allah to settle their disputes”** means that they were called to let revelation decide between them. Al-Suddī reports that al-Nuʿmān ibn Awfā asked the Prophet ﷺ to let their rabbis judge a dispute. The Prophet ﷺ instead called for Allah’s Book to be the judge, but they refused.

Another report, related from Ibn ʿAbbās by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah, says that the Prophet ﷺ entered a Jewish place of study and called its people to Allah. Nuʿaym ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḥārith ibn Zayd asked what religion he followed. He answered that he followed the religion of Ibrāhīm (Abraham). They claimed that Ibrāhīm had been Jewish. The Prophet ﷺ suggested that they consult the Torah to decide the matter, but they refused.

Al-Kalbī connects the dispute to a case of adultery at Khaybar. The Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ for a ruling. He gave the judgment that was found in their own Torah, but they were angry and some refused to accept it. One account says they were called to apply the punishment of stoning for a married man and woman. One account says the fuller discussion of this legal ruling appears later in al-Māʾidah. These reports differ in their immediate occasion, but they share the same point: the people who claimed the scripture turned away when its ruling challenged them.

**“some of them turn away heedlessly”** describes refusal, not ignorance. They did not want to accept the judgment and its consequences. The verse censures people who ask for a ruling but reject it when it does not match their desires.

An inward reading says that the call itself tests people whose refusal is already known to Allah. Their turning away reflects deprivation from the beauty of divine disclosure. The Prophet ﷺ is told to remain patient with the task given to him and to recognize the state of those who refuse.

### Why did they refuse the Book’s judgment?

The accounts give more than one setting, including a dispute about religious identity and a legal case. In each, the Torah is offered as the standard, yet some of those who claim to follow it resist its ruling. The issue is not a lack of access to scripture. It is their unwillingness to accept a judgment that conflicts with their preference.

### In short

- The verse criticizes people who claimed to follow scripture but turned away when asked to accept its judgment.
- Reports connect the refusal with disputes over Abraham’s religion and with a legal ruling found in the Torah.
- The inward reading treats their refusal as a test and calls the Prophet ﷺ to patience.

24.text:
The verse explains their confidence in turning away: “The Fire will not touch us except for a few days” (3:24). They believed punishment would be brief, then treated themselves as safe. The explanations describe this claim as something they had invented without authority. Their false assurance deceived them and made them bold in rejecting truth.

### Phrase by phrase

**“This is because they say”** introduces the claim. **“The Fire will not touch us except for a few days”** (3:24) refers to their belief that any punishment would be short. One explanation says they believed they would remain in the Fire for seven days, one day for each thousand years of earthly life. Another says they tied the punishment to the forty days their ancestors worshipped the calf. A further account describes them saying they would be punished for only a limited number of days. These are reported versions of the claim, not a statement that the claim is true.

Some held that they were protected because they were descendants of prophets. Others said the punishment would be delayed. The explanations present these beliefs as invented assurances that had no authority from Allah. Their false expectation made them feel secure even while rejecting revelation.

**“They have been deceived in their faith by their wishful lying”** means that the claim itself misled them. They were not relying on a promise Allah had made. They had fabricated the idea that punishment would soon end and then allowed it to reassure them. An inward reading says that they were drawn gradually into greater false confidence, until they presumed they could set the limits of their own punishment. They would eventually discover that their affliction would be increased, not reduced.

### In short

- The people described claimed that punishment in the Fire would last only a short time.
- Explanations give different versions of the number of days and the reason they expected brief punishment.
- The verse calls this belief a deception they invented, not a promise from Allah.

25.text:
The verse asks the people who believed they were safe to consider the Day “about which there is no doubt” (3:25). Allah will gather them, repay each soul in full for what it has done, and wrong no one. The imagined limit they placed on punishment cannot change the reality of the final judgment.

### Phrase by phrase

**“But how ˹horrible˺ will it be”** expresses the gravity of what awaits them. **“when We gather them together on the Day”** points to the Day of Resurrection. **“about which there is no doubt”** (3:25) affirms that it is certain to come. The people who denied revelation and rejected the messengers will be gathered with everyone else, and their claims about escaping punishment will be exposed. One explanation asks what their condition will be after their lies about Allah, their rejection of messengers, and their killing of prophets and those who called for righteousness are brought to account.

An inward reading describes the Day as so imposing that the minds of those who turned away will be bewildered and their claims cut off. They will face accounting, reproach (ʿitāb), punishment, and the absence of honor and approval (ʿadam al-ikrām). Another mystical distinction says that the gathering of all people for judgment is in the future, while the gathering of those who love Allah occurs in the present moment.

**“when every soul will be paid in full for what it has done”** means that each person receives the full consequence of good and evil actions. Nothing is overlooked, and no one can substitute an invented promise for the account of what they actually did.

**“and none will be wronged”** means that good deeds will not be reduced and sins will not be increased. Allah’s judgment is just. Every person receives what is due without injustice.

### What does full recompense mean?

The verse leaves no room for an assumed exception. A person’s own actions will be weighed, and no one can claim that a small set of days or an inherited status makes the final account irrelevant. Justice means that good is not reduced and evil is not increased.

### In short

- All people will be gathered for a certain Day of Resurrection.
- Each soul will receive the full recompense for its deeds.
- No good deed will be reduced, no sin increased, and no one will be wronged.

26.text:
The verse teaches the Prophet ﷺ and the believers to pray, “O Allah! Lord over all authorities!” Allah alone gives and removes authority, honors and disgraces whom He wills, and holds all good in His hands. The prayer reminds believers that the rise and fall of nations is not decided by human power alone. It also answers those who mocked the promise that the Muslim community would reach lands then ruled by powerful empires.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘O Allah! Lord over all authorities!’”** teaches praise, gratitude, reliance, and trust. The word Allāhumma means “O Allah.” An inward explanation notes that the final mīm serves in place of the ordinary word used to call someone. The phrase recognizes Allah as the sole owner of sovereignty, with no partner, helper, companion, or rival in rule or creation.

The verse was revealed in a setting where the Prophet ﷺ promised that the Byzantine and Persian lands would come under Muslim rule. The Jews and hypocrites mocked the promise. One report places the words after the conquest of Makkah, when people doubted that Muhammad ﷺ and his community could overcome Persia and Byzantium. Another relates them to al-Ahzab, the Battle of the Confederates, called Khandaq, the Trench, in historical accounts. This followed the disbelievers’ defeats at Badr and Uhud and the growing strength of the Muslims. Arabia’s disbelievers, Jews, and Christians joined together to attack Madinah, and the Prophet’s Companions dug a trench.

In one account, ten men were assigned forty hand-spans of trench, which was several miles long, deep, and wide. Another report describes ten men assigned a forty-cubit stretch. The Companions worked without stopping and on hungry stomachs, with little time even for pressing needs. The Prophet ﷺ worked beside them, and the task was described as difficult even for a modern army engineering team. When the diggers met a hard rock they could not break, Salmān al-Fārisī went to ask him for help. The Prophet ﷺ struck the rock three times. Each strike produced a flash of light. In the first, he said he saw the palaces of Ḥīrah in Persia. In the second, he saw the red palaces of the Byzantines. In the third, he saw the palaces of Ṣanʿāʾ in Yemen. He gave the Companions the news that their ummah, the Muslim community, would prevail in those lands. When the hypocrites heard this, they mocked the hungry workers who were unsure of their own safety but spoke of conquering distant powers. The verse came as an answer and a prayer affirming that all authority belongs to Allah.

Reports about the trench are attributed to al-Baihaqi, Abu Nu'aim, and Ibn Khuzaimah. Another account from Ibn ʿAbbās and Anas ibn Mālik connects the verse to the promise of Persia and Byzantium after Makkah was conquered. A report from Qatādah says that the Prophet ﷺ asked Allah to grant those kingdoms to his community.

**“You give authority to whoever You please and remove it from who You please”** means that sovereignty belongs to Allah. He gives it to one person or people and takes it from others. Human rulers cannot secure it against His will. The Qur’an rejects the assumption that people can decide who should receive Allah’s mercy and prophethood. It asks whether they would distribute their Lord’s mercy themselves (43:31, 43:32), and says Allah knows best where to place His message (6:124). People are also favored differently in this life (17:21).

One explanation says this verse foretells that prophethood would pass from the Children of Israel to an Arab, Qurayshi, Makkan, unlettered prophet, Muhammad ﷺ, the final messenger to humankind and jinn. Allah gave him knowledge of His law and of past and future events. The Muslim community would spread east and west, including Persia, Byzantium, Syria, Iraq, and Yemen, and the religion and law he brought would prevail over other religions and laws. This is presented as Allah’s gift, not as a power the community could claim for itself.

**“You honour whoever You please and disgrace whoever You please”** continues the same point. Allah can raise the poor and humble and remove honor from rulers. One report applies the humiliation to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and the people of Persia and Byzantium. Another connects it to Quraysh, who asked why the Qur’an had not been sent to a great man from Makkah or Ṭāʾif (43:31). The answer is that Allah distributes His mercy and chooses whom He wills, not those whom people consider most powerful.

**“all good is in Your Hands”** says that Allah’s acts are good in the wider order of creation. The verse names both giving and removing authority, and both honoring and disgracing, yet it says that all good is in Allah’s hands. An explanation says an event can be unwelcome to one person or nation but serve a wider good for others. The loss of one group may become a gain for another. The poet al-Mutanabbī expressed this as one group’s calamity becoming another’s benefit. The statement does not deny that a person may experience something painful. It places that experience within Allah’s complete wisdom and knowledge.

**“Surely You ˹alone˺ are Most Capable of everything”** confirms that no person can resist Allah’s decision. He can raise the weak to honor and remove power from kings. He can fulfill what appears impossible to people.

### What does the inward reading add?

An allusive reading treats the prayer as a lesson in how to praise Allah. He has no partner in His essence, kingdom, creation, or power. Created beings find honor by humbling themselves before Him. Allah raises whom He wills by drawing them near, enabling them to witness His oneness, and occupying their hearts with Him. He lowers whom He wills by leaving them to distraction and the clamor of the lower self. In this reading, true honor is nearness to Allah, and true disgrace is estrangement from Him. The honor or ʿizz of the servant lies in humility and self-effacement (maḥw). Lasting life (baqā) comes through the surrender and passing away (fanā) of the lower self. The first gleams of intimacy, called ṭawāliʿ, raise a person toward Allah. The night visitors of the lower self, ṭawāriq, pull the person toward distraction.

### In short

- Allah alone gives and removes authority and bestows honor or disgrace.
- The verse is linked to promises about the Muslim community’s future and to the mocking of those promises.
- The trench account describes the Prophet ﷺ receiving visions of Persian, Byzantine, and Yemeni palaces after striking a rock.
- Even painful changes in power are within Allah’s wisdom, and true honor is nearness to Him.

27.text:
The verse says, “You cause the night to pass into the day and the day into the night.” It presents the changing night and day, life emerging from what appears dead, and the provision Allah gives as signs of His complete power. The same power that governs the world also guides human hearts and changes their states.

### Phrase by phrase

**“You cause the night to pass into the day and the day into the night”** means that Allah lengthens one and shortens the other. The change unfolds across the seasons as the balance between daylight and darkness shifts. The power that governs the heavens and the cycles of time belongs to Allah alone.

**“You bring forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living”** has several examples. A chick comes from an egg, and an egg from a bird. A plant grows from a seed, and a seed comes from a plant. A human being develops from a drop, and a drop comes from a living person. Dates emerge from their seeds and seeds from dates. The phrase can also describe spiritual change: Allah can bring a believer from a disbelieving family or a disbeliever from a believing one. He brought Ibrāhīm (Abraham) from people who worshipped idols, while the son of Nūḥ (Noah) remained an unbeliever. A scholar’s child may be ignorant, and a child of an unlearned person may become learned. Allah can change the state of faith or knowledge as He wills.

Another inward reading treats night passing into day as the light of tawhid, the oneness of Allah, overcoming the darkness of the lower self. Day passing into night can describe the heart’s light being eclipsed by the lower self. The living emerging from the dead can represent hope and renewed closeness after spiritual apathy. The dead emerging from the living can describe a heart that becomes barren after rejecting faith. A verse about those who did not believe the first time is cited in this connection (6:110).

**“And You provide for whoever You will without limit”** means that Allah grants provision in abundance to some and restricts it for others, with wisdom and justice. Provision can mean wealth and sustenance, given without measure or strain. The verse describes Allah’s power to provide beyond what people can calculate. A messenger of truth may lose a home or material support, yet Allah can provide special help without measure.

A report about the merit of these verses says that a person who recites Al-Fātiḥah, Ayat al-Kursi, verse 3:18, and the present verses after each surah will be given a home in Paradise, placed in the Sacred Enclosure, receive mercy seventy times each day, have seventy needs fulfilled, and be protected from every envier and enemy. The report is presented as a promise of Allah’s care and aid.

### How does this power reach the human soul?

The verse moves from the cycles of the heavens to changes in faith, knowledge, and provision. Allah can bring a believer out of an unbelieving family, or allow a believer’s child to reject faith. He can make a learned person from someone uneducated or reverse that state. These examples show that neither belief, knowledge, nor provision lies beyond His control. The inward reading also treats the alternation of night and day as changes in the heart, from light and closeness to darkness and distance.

### In short

- Allah controls the passage of night and day and all changes in the natural world.
- He brings life from what appears dead and can also change spiritual states, bringing a believer from disbelief or allowing a person to turn away.
- He provides without limit and gives support beyond what people can calculate.

28.text:
The verse warns, “Believers should not take disbelievers as guardians instead of the believers.” It concerns loyalty and deep emotional friendship, not every kind of contact with non-Muslims. One explanation identifies hypocrites around ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy as an immediate example of this danger. The explanations distinguish intimate bonds that oppose the faith from kindness, courtesy, and ordinary dealings. If believers face a real threat, they may protect themselves outwardly while keeping their inward faith.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Believers should not take disbelievers as guardians instead of the believers”** forbids close loyalty that places those who oppose faith above the believing community. The warning is repeated elsewhere in the Qur’an. It cautions against choosing disbelievers as protectors instead of believers (4:144), names Jews and Christians in a particular warning about taking them as close allies (5:51), and recalls that enemies and their allies can bring fitnah, disorder, and corruption (8:73). Another passage says that those who make enemies of Allah and His Messenger cannot be found among people who truly believe in Allah and the Last Day, even if the enemies are close relatives (58:22).

One explanation says the prohibited relationship is muwālāt, an intimate bond of affection and loyal support. This close bond is described as ḥarām, forbidden. This kind of friendship joins a person’s heart to another’s cause. It is different from showing kindness, sympathy, hospitality, or fairness. The explanation also distinguishes muwāsāt, benevolent concern and practical support, from mudārāt, courteous and tactful conduct. Both can be shown to non-Muslims who are not fighting the Muslims. The verse does not prohibit justice, compassion, or ordinary courtesy.

**“and whoever does so will have nothing to hope for from Allah”** warns that a person who chooses the prohibited loyalty risks losing Allah’s protection and mercy. Another verse says that whoever takes Allah’s enemies as friends has strayed from the straight path (60:1). The warning is serious because this kind of allegiance can undermine the purpose of faith.

**“unless it is a precaution against their tyranny”** gives an exception for a person who fears real danger. A believer in a place or time of threat may use friendly words or outward behavior to protect life, while not giving the heart’s allegiance to the enemy. Abū al-Dardāʾ is reported to have said that they smiled at some people while their hearts rejected them. Al-Bukhārī recorded this report. Al-Ḥasan said that protective dissimulation remains permitted when safety requires it. The exception concerns outward self-protection, not inward loyalty.

Surah al-Mumtaḥanah also says that Allah does not forbid kindness and justice toward people who do not fight believers over faith or drive them from their homes (60:8). The warnings in al-Mumtaḥanah (60:1) and al-Mujādilah (58:22) concern hostile allegiance, not basic fairness. This supports the distinction between intimate allegiance and humane conduct. Trade, employment, hospitality, condolences, charity, and ordinary dealings are treated differently from close friendship that would compromise faith or harm the Muslim community.

**“And Allah warns you about Himself”** warns against His anger and punishment for supporting those who oppose His friends. The verse calls believers to examine what their loyalties mean and where they lead.

**“And to Allah is the final return”** reminds everyone that all people return to Allah, who will reward or punish them according to their deeds.

### What kinds of relations are distinguished?

The explanations set out several levels. Close emotional loyalty and intimate friendship are restricted to believers. Sympathy, kindness, charity, consolation, and wishing others well are permitted with people who are not at war with the Muslims. Polite and cordial behavior is also permitted, especially when welcoming a guest, explaining the faith, or avoiding harm. Trade and other practical dealings are allowed unless they injure the wider community. One legal example forbids selling arms to those actively fighting Muslims while permitting ordinary trade and employment.

The reports describe the Prophet ﷺ showing compassion to non-Muslims. During famine in Makkah, he helped people who had forced him to leave his home. After the city came under his control, he forgave those who had persecuted him and said they would not be blamed for their past treatment. He treated prisoners tenderly. A delegation from Thaqīf that had not yet accepted Islam was allowed to stay in the Prophet’s Mosque. ʿUmar also gave support to needy non-Muslim residents. These examples are presented as kindness, courtesy, and practical care, not as the intimate allegiance forbidden by the verse.

### Why is intimate loyalty treated differently?

The explanation presents life as having a central purpose: remembering and serving the Creator. Rūmī is quoted as saying, in effect, that life without devotion to the Creator is empty and shameful. Business, government, family, and social ties should serve that purpose rather than replace it. The Qur’an says that Satan is an enemy and should be treated as one (35:6), and that a believer’s prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are for Allah, Lord of the Worlds (6:162). People whose cause opposes this purpose cannot be made the object of a believer’s deepest loyalty.

A hadith recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim says that a person’s faith is perfected through loving and opposing for Allah’s sake. An inward reading says that true friendship means aligning oneself with Allah’s friends and opposing the enmity directed at them. It tells of an earlier prophet being instructed to ask people what they had done for Allah, beyond seeking their own comfort and reputation. Another report recounts ʿĪsā (Jesus) being told that worship alone would not benefit someone who had no love for Allah’s friends and no opposition to His enemies.

Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī told Muʿādh that he loved him for Allah’s sake. Muʿādh replied with good news and reported that the Prophet ﷺ described people who love one another for Allah’s sake as being given seats near the Throne. Others will fear the Resurrection, while they are safe. Another report says Allah’s love is promised to people who love, sit with, visit, and spend for one another for His sake. Mujāhid said that the sins of Allah’s friends fall away when they smile at each other.

### In short

- The verse prohibits intimate loyalty that places opposition to faith above the believing community.
- It does not prohibit kindness, fairness, hospitality, trade, employment, or courtesy toward non-Muslims who are not fighting believers.
- A person facing real danger may protect themselves outwardly while keeping faith inwardly.
- The Prophet ﷺ and the early community are described as treating non-Muslims with mercy and generosity while maintaining the distinction between kindness and intimate allegiance.

29.text:
The verse says, “Whether you conceal what is in your hearts or reveal it, it is known to Allah.” It follows the warning about loyalty by reminding believers that Allah knows what they hide as well as what they show. Nothing in the heavens or earth lies outside His knowledge or power.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺”** directs Muhammad ﷺ to make this declaration openly.

**“Whether you conceal what is in your hearts or reveal it”** includes hidden loyalties, hostility, and intentions as well as words and visible actions. One explanation applies it to concealed affection for disbelievers or open hostility toward Muhammad ﷺ. Another says that secret hatred, public abuse, and even preparations for war are all known to Allah. A person cannot make a false claim about what is in the heart and expect it to remain hidden from Him.

**“it is known to Allah”** means that Allah knows secret and public matters, in every condition and at every time. Not even the weight of an atom, or what is smaller, escapes His knowledge in the earth, seas, mountains, or heavens.

**“For He knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth”** restates the reach of His knowledge. Nothing a person conceals is outside the knowledge of the One who knows all creation.

**“And Allah is Most Capable of everything”** warns that Allah can punish wrongdoing and can do all that He wills. His knowledge is not passive. He is able to act on what He knows.

An inward reading uses this assurance to comfort the believer during hardship. No calamity escapes Allah’s knowledge. He can bring help and a response, and trials will pass by His will.

### In short

- Allah knows what people hide and what they reveal.
- His knowledge reaches everything in the heavens and earth, including the smallest thing.
- He has power to respond to what He knows, and the believer can trust that no hardship is outside His care.

30.text:
The verse warns of “the Day when every soul will be presented with whatever good it has done.” Each person will also see the evil they committed and wish it were far away. Allah warns people about His punishment, yet the verse ends by describing Him as gracious to His servants. It joins fear of wrongdoing with hope in His mercy.

### Phrase by phrase

**“˹Watch for˺ the Day”** points to the Day of Resurrection. It is a day when deeds are brought before each person, not merely remembered in the mind.

**“when every soul will be presented with whatever good it has done”** means a person will see good deeds made present. Seeing them brings happiness and relief.

**“And it will wish that its misdeeds were far off”** describes the distress of seeing evil actions. A person will want distance between themselves and those deeds. The wish is not a way to undo what happened. One verse describes someone wishing the distance between them and their former companion were as far as the two easts (43:38). Another says that each person will be told what they sent ahead and what they left behind (75:13).

**“And Allah warns you about Himself”** repeats the warning so people do not ignore the consequences of disobedience. An inward reading says this severity can throw the servant into fear, confusion, and a sense of self-loss.

**“And Allah is Ever Gracious to ˹His˺ servants”** restores hope. Allah’s kindness does not cancel the warning. It gives the servant a way back and prevents despair. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that Allah is kind to people by warning them about Himself. Another inward reading pictures Allah seating the servant on a ship of gentleness and carrying them from the whirlpool of confusion to the shore of intimacy.

A spiritual teacher asks whether the heart will ever escape the whirlpool of self and whether compassion will guide it through the waves of desire. The reflection describes a person caught between fear and hope, contraction and openness, harshness and generosity. The warning awakens the person to the danger of wrongdoing. The promise of kindness keeps that warning from becoming despair.

### How can warning and mercy stand together?

The warning calls people to take their choices seriously. The promise of kindness assures them that Allah’s purpose is not to leave them without guidance. Together they create a balance: fear restrains disobedience, while hope in mercy encourages repentance and return.

### In short

- Every soul will see its good and evil deeds on the Day of Resurrection.
- People will wish to be far from their misdeeds, but that wish will not erase them.
- Allah warns against disobedience and is also gracious to His servants, joining fear with hope.

31.text:
The Prophet ﷺ is told to say, “If you ˹sincerely˺ love Allah, then follow me.” The verse gives a test for a claim that cannot be measured by words alone. Love of Allah must lead to following Muhammad ﷺ. The result is Allah’s love and forgiveness.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺”** makes Muhammad ﷺ the one who delivers the test of sincere love.

**“If you ˹sincerely˺ love Allah, then follow me”** means that the person who claims love must follow the Prophet ﷺ in belief, actions, and conduct. The way he brought is the measure of the claim. A hadith says that an action not in accordance with the Prophet’s religion will be rejected. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and other early scholars said that people claimed to love Allah, so Allah tested them with this verse. Love is hidden, but following the messenger is visible.

An inward reading urges the seeker to walk in the Prophet’s footsteps rather than let unaided intellect set the path. Intellect can guard and assess, but the religious way is learned from prophethood. It says the religion shared by the 124,000 prophets and messengers, from Nūḥ (Noah), Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Mūsā (Moses), and ʿĪsā to Muhammad ﷺ, is submission to Allah (42:13). It rests on what Allah says and what His Messenger says, not on speculation that conflicts with revelation. The Qur’an says that Allah completed the religion (5:3).

A mystical account says that before the world and Adam were created, the spirits of the prophets made a covenant to follow the messenger who would come. The account then describes Adam, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus coming and passing, until Muhammad ﷺ was given the final mission and the covenant was reaffirmed (3:81). It says that at his coming, fourteen battlements fell from Caesar’s fortress and the idols in the Kaaba fell face-down. The image is paired with the promise that truth has come and falsehood has vanished (17:81). This is presented as an allusive account of the final messenger’s place, not as a new historical report.

**“Allah will love you”** promises more than the human claim that begins the verse. If people follow the Prophet ﷺ, Allah will love them. An inward reading connects “you love Allah” with seeking, and “Allah will love you” with the closeness that comes when He responds. It also speaks of the path of the Tariqah, the spiritual way, as a movement from separation toward nearness.

**“and forgive your sins”** promises pardon through the blessing of the Prophet’s mission and through repentance. One explanation says that those who repent are forgiven for earlier sins.

**“For Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”** gives hope to those who return and follow the Prophet ﷺ. Allah’s forgiveness is not a reason to make a false claim of love. It is the mercy promised to those who turn to Him.

### How can love be tested?

A person cannot directly measure love by looking inside the heart. The verse gives an outward test: whether the person follows the Prophet ﷺ and lives by the guidance he brought. Stronger claims of love should lead to stronger obedience. The verse therefore joins belief in Allah’s oneness with belief in prophethood and following the messenger.

### In short

- A claim of love for Allah is tested by following Muhammad ﷺ.
- Following the Prophet brings Allah’s love and forgiveness.
- The prophetic way, not speculation that contradicts revelation, is the guide to obedience.

32.text:
The verse commands, “Obey Allah and His Messenger.” It makes obedience the response to the call of love in the previous verse. If people turn away from Allah’s command and the Prophet’s way, the verse says that Allah does not love the disbelievers.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺”** tells Muhammad ﷺ to deliver this command.

**“Obey Allah and His Messenger”** means to follow Allah’s instructions and avoid His prohibitions, including the call to worship Him alone. It includes following the Prophet’s practices and the sacred law he brought. The verse makes clear that love is not simply a feeling. It requires obedience. One explanation calls deliberate defiance of the Messenger’s way kufr, disbelief, because it rejects the message he brought.

**“If they still turn away”** describes those who refuse the command or fall short by opposing it.

**“then truly Allah does not like the disbelievers”** names persistent refusal as disbelief, not merely a failure to perform one act. An inward explanation notes that the verse says “disbelievers,” not simply “disobedient people.” It also leaves open that Allah may love believers who have sinned, even while their actions are wrong. The verse warns those who reject the message and do not obey the Messenger.

### In short

- The response to love for Allah is obedience to Allah and His Messenger.
- Turning away from the message is described as disbelief.
- The verse distinguishes rejection of faith from the sins of a person who still believes.

33.text:
The verse says, “Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ’Imrân” (3:33). It describes selected people and households whom Allah raised above others of their time. The next verses turn to the family of ʿImrān and the birth and upbringing of Maryam (Mary).

### Phrase by phrase

**“Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah”** names two prophets selected for their missions. Adam was created by Allah, taught the names of things, and given a place in Paradise before being sent down according to divine wisdom. Allah commanded the angels to bow before him. Nūḥ (Noah) was made a messenger to people who worshipped idols. He called them openly and privately for a long period, but many turned further away. He prayed against them, and Allah drowned those who rejected him. Those who followed the religion sent to Nūḥ were saved.

**“the family of Abraham”** includes the prophet Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and his descendants. One explanation says the family was chosen because prophethood continued among them, including Muhammad ﷺ, the final prophet.

**“and the family of ’Imrân”** refers here to the family of Maryam and her son ʿĪsā (Jesus). One explanation identifies ʿImrān as Mary’s father. Another explanation distinguishes this ʿImrān from the person associated with Mūsā (Moses) and Hārūn (Aaron). The verse introduces the account of Maryam, whose birth and upbringing are described next.

**“above all people ˹of their time˺”** means Allah favored these people and households over others of their age by choosing them for prophethood and guidance. The wording does not say that their status came automatically through family descent. An inward reading says that being chosen is a gift from Allah, not something inherited merely through lineage.

### Why are these households named together?

The verse links Adam, Nūḥ, Ibrāhīm’s family, and ʿImrān’s family as people chosen to carry guidance. One explanation says that the names were also a comfort to Muhammad ﷺ when people doubted his prophethood. The passage is about Allah’s choice and the prophets’ mission, while the family of ʿImrān leads directly into the account of Maryam and ʿĪsā.

### In short

- Allah chose Adam, Nūḥ, the family of Ibrāhīm, and the family of ʿImrān above people of their time.
- Their distinction came through Allah’s choice and prophethood, not simply through ancestry.
- The mention of ʿImrān introduces the story of Maryam and ʿĪsā.

34.text:
The verse says, “They are descendants of one another” (3:34). It links the chosen people in the previous verse through family descent and a shared way of worshipping Allah. Their message centers on Allah’s oneness and doing what is right. Allah hears what people say and knows their actions.

### Phrase by phrase

**“They are descendants of one another”** can mean that some were ancestors of others and that the chosen households were connected through family lines. It also points to continuity in their faith and conduct. The prophets and their followers called people to worship Allah alone and to do good.

An inward explanation says that sharing descent does not itself make a person chosen. Being selected is something Allah grants, not an automatic result of kinship. Another explanation says that people in these families passed noble character and virtue from one generation to another.

**“And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”** means He hears what people say and knows what they do and intend. He knows who follows His way and who only claims a connection to those He chose.

### In short

- The chosen people are connected by descent and by a shared call to Allah’s oneness.
- Family connection alone does not guarantee that a person is chosen.
- Allah hears people’s claims and knows their actions and intentions.

35.text:
The verse recalls the prayer of the wife of ʿImrān: “My Lord! I dedicate what is in my womb entirely to Your service” (3:35). She vows that her child will be devoted to worship and service at the sacred place in Jerusalem. She asks Allah to accept the vow, knowing that He hears prayer and knows her intention.

### Phrase by phrase

**“˹Remember˺ when the wife of ’Imrân said”** introduces the mother of Maryam. One report gives her name as Ḥannah bint Fāqūdh. She had been unable to have children and prayed to Allah after seeing a bird feeding its young. Allah granted her a child. Muhammad bin Ishaq relates this account of Hannah, the wife of ʿImrān. She made the vow while pregnant, not yet knowing whether she would give birth to a boy or a girl. Her husband ʿImrān died while she was still pregnant, according to one report.

**“My Lord! I dedicate what is in my womb entirely to Your service”** describes a vow to free the child from ordinary worldly work and devote the child to worship and service at Bayt al-Maqdis, the sacred place in Jerusalem. In the religious practice described for earlier prophets, a child could be dedicated to this service. The mother expected a boy, whom she thought would be able to fulfill the role.

An inward reading understands the consecrated person as someone freed from being occupied by created things and devoted wholly to Allah. It says that the mother’s vow expressed sincerity, even though she did not know the child’s sex or what the child’s future would be.

**“so accept it from me”** is a request that Allah receive the vow. The mother does not assume that her intention alone guarantees acceptance. She asks for it as a gift.

**“You ˹alone˺ are truly the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”** recognizes that Allah hears the prayer and knows what is in the womb and the intention behind the vow. She asks the One who knows her purpose to accept it.

### The child’s later dedication and the Sunnah of naming

The surrounding account also discusses what happens after a child is born. The Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ includes naming a newborn on the day of birth. Al-Bukhari and Muslim report that the Prophet said a son had been born to him and that he named him Ibrāhīm, after his father. They also report that Anas brought his newborn brother to the Prophet, who softened a date, placed some in the baby’s mouth, and named him ʿAbd Allāh. These reports show that a child can be named promptly, alongside the mother’s earlier dedication and prayer.

A report from Qatādah, from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, from Samurah bin Jundub describes the ʿaqīqah: a newborn boy is connected to a sacrifice on his behalf until the seventh day, when he is named and his hair is shaved. Aḥmad and the compilers of the Sunan collections recorded the report, and At-Tirmidhi graded it ṣaḥīḥ. Another narration says that blood is offered on his behalf. The explanation notes that this wording is more famous and established than the wording that simply says a sacrifice is offered. These are later practices concerning a newborn, distinct from the mother’s vow to dedicate the child to service at Bayt al-Maqdis.

### In short

- The wife of ʿImrān prayed for a child and vowed to dedicate the child to worship and service in Jerusalem.
- She made the vow while pregnant and did not yet know she would give birth to a girl.
- She asked Allah to accept the vow because He hears prayer and knows intention.

36.text:
The verse records the mother’s response: “My Lord! I have given birth to a girl” (3:36). She had hoped for a boy who could serve at the sacred place, so she expresses her surprise. She names the child Maryam and asks Allah to protect her and her offspring from Satan.

### Phrase by phrase

**“When she delivered, she said, ‘My Lord! I have given birth to a girl’”** shows that the child was not what her mother expected. The explanation says she thought a boy would be better suited to the dedicated service because of differences in strength and the effects of menstruation. In that earlier religious practice, only boys were expected to serve in this way. The verse then says that Allah knew best what she had delivered, marking Allah’s knowledge of Maryam’s future and honor.

**“and the male is not like the female”** records the mother’s understanding of the difference in suitability for the particular service she had vowed. An inward reading says that, outwardly, a boy and girl differ, but Allah accepted Maryam and made signs and miracles appear through her and her son. Her being a girl did not prevent Allah from honoring her beyond what her mother had imagined.

**“I have named her Mary”** gives the child her name. The passage is also cited as evidence that a mother may name her child and that a name may be given on the day of birth. The mother’s vow concerns the child’s upbringing and dedication, and one explanation says that a mother has a measure of guardianship over that education and training.

**“and I seek Your protection for her and her offspring from Satan, the accursed”** is the mother’s prayer for Maryam and her descendants. She asks Allah to protect them from Satan’s evil. One report from Abū Hurayrah says that every newborn is touched by Satan and begins crying, except Maryam and her son ʿĪsā. ʿAbd al-Razzāq recorded the report. It is presented as an answer to the mother’s request for protection.

### What does the mother’s response teach?

The mother’s surprise does not mean her prayer was rejected. She made the vow sincerely, and Allah knew what the child would become. One inward reading says that Maryam’s acceptance produced signs that would not have appeared if the child’s sex had been the only measure of her suitability. The mother continues to entrust Maryam and her descendants to Allah’s protection.

### Other teachings connected with birth

Muhammad bin Ishaq’s account identifies the mother as Hannah, wife of ʿImrān. The reports surrounding this birth also discuss the Sunnah of naming a child. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, the Two Sahihs, record that the Prophet named a son Ibrāhīm after his father. They also relate that Anas brought his newborn brother, whom the Prophet named ʿAbd Allāh. These reports are distinct from the mother’s naming of Maryam, but they support naming a child at birth.

Another report, transmitted from Qatādah through al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī from Samurah bin Jundub, discusses ʿaqīqah. It says that a newborn boy is tied to a sacrifice on his behalf until the seventh day, when he is named and his hair is shaved. Aḥmad and the compilers of the Sunan recorded it, and At-Tirmidhi graded it ṣaḥīḥ. An alternate wording says that blood is offered on his behalf and is described as the more famous, established version. These teachings explain practices related to a child’s birth, while the verse itself emphasizes Maryam’s name and the mother’s supplication.

### In short

- The mother expected a boy but gave birth to Maryam, a girl.
- She named Maryam and asked Allah to protect her and her descendants from Satan.
- Allah knew Maryam’s future and accepted her dedication despite her mother’s surprise.

37.text:
The verse says, “So her Lord accepted her graciously and blessed her with a pleasant upbringing” (3:37). Allah accepts the mother’s dedication of Maryam, cares for her, and appoints Zakariyyā (Zachariah) as her guardian. At the place of worship, Zakariyyā finds her supplied with food that appears outside its season. Maryam says that it comes from Allah, who provides without limit.

### Phrase by phrase

**“So her Lord accepted her graciously”** means that Allah received Maryam and her mother’s dedication with favor. One explanation says He accepted her in place of the boy her mother expected. He made her beloved among people and caused the righteous to care for her. An inward reading says that Allah’s gracious acceptance kept Maryam preserved and obedient, even though people would later say hurtful things because of her and her son.

**“and blessed her with a pleasant upbringing”** means that Allah gave Maryam excellent character and guided her to knowledge, religion, and righteous conduct. One report describes her as growing unusually quickly. Another explains the phrase as Allah nurturing her throughout every stage of life and hour.

**“entrusting her to the care of Zachariah”** describes Zakariyyā becoming Maryam’s guardian. Her mother brought her to the caretakers and worshippers at Bayt al-Maqdis and told them of her vow. They wanted custody because ʿImrān, Maryam’s father, had been a leader at the sanctuary. Some explanations say Zakariyyā was the husband of Maryam’s maternal aunt. Another describes him as her brother-in-law. A hadith in the two major collections compares the maternal aunt to a mother, supporting the closeness of the relationship.

The people did not agree at first, so they drew lots. One report says twenty-nine caretakers cast their pens into the Jordan. They agreed that the pen which remained steady and rose to the surface would identify the guardian. Zakariyyā’s pen did so, and he took charge of Maryam. Another account says her mother asked the caretakers to take her in, Zakariyyā argued that he was best suited because his wife was her aunt, and the group resolved the dispute by lots.

Zakariyyā arranged a private room for Maryam near the sanctuary, where she could worship. Some reports say he arranged for a wet nurse. Others say that Maryam did not need one. The explanations differ on these details, while agreeing that she grew under his care.

**“Whenever Zachariah visited her in the sanctuary, he found her supplied with provisions”** describes a sign of Allah’s care. Zakariyyā would find Maryam provided with food. The explanations say that she received summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer. One account says that Gabriel brought the food to her.

**“He exclaimed, ‘O Mary! Where did this come from?’”** shows Zakariyyā’s surprise at the provision and his question about its origin.

**“She replied, ‘It is from Allah’”** gives Maryam’s answer. She does not claim the food as her own achievement. She recognizes Allah as its giver.

**“Surely Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit”** means that Allah gives freely, beyond ordinary measure or seasonal expectation. The provision at the sanctuary shows His care for Maryam and His ability to provide as He wills.

### Reports that explain the guardianship and provision

Muhammad bin Ishaq and Ibn Jarir both report that Zakariyyā was married to Maryam’s maternal aunt. Another report describes him as her brother-in-law. A report about the relationship between Yaḥyā (John) and ʿĪsā says they were maternal cousins. The Two Sahihs also preserve the Prophet’s ruling about ʿAmārah, daughter of Ḥamzah: she was placed with her maternal aunt, the wife of Jaʿfar bin Abi Talib, and he said that a maternal aunt is like a mother. These reports are cited to explain the closeness of Maryam’s aunt and Zakariyyā and why he was a suitable guardian.

The account of the lots is given in more than one form. In one telling, the caretakers cast their pens in the Jordan and agreed that the one which stayed firm and surfaced would identify Maryam’s guardian. Zakariyyā’s pen did so. In another telling, those who served at the sanctuary first disputed who should care for Maryam, then agreed that lots would settle the matter. Both versions place the decision in Allah’s care rather than presenting Zakariyyā as taking custody by force.

Several early interpreters explain the unusual food as seasonal fruit appearing at the opposite time of year. The account names al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ bin Anas, and al-Suddī, as well as Mujāhid, Abū Ash-Shaʿthāʾ, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, and ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī among those who reported this. One account says Gabriel brought it. The word miḥrāb here means the sanctuary or worship room where Maryam stayed. An inward reading says she could be found there, devoted to worship, and that her excellent upbringing included ḥusn, excellence of character, and ʿiṣma, protection from sin and error. It connects this protection with Maryam’s request for refuge in the Compassionate One (19:18), and with the righteous fruit of her story, ʿĪsā.

A saying attributed to Dāwūd (David) advises: “If you see someone seeking Me, become a servant to him.” The word ṭāliban means a seeker. The saying is used to illustrate Zakariyyā’s service to Maryam as one who sought Allah. These reflections portray her care as a responsibility and honor, not merely a dispute over custody.

### Why was Zakariyyā chosen as her guardian?

The explanations differ about his exact family relationship to Maryam. Some say he was married to her maternal aunt, while another calls him her brother-in-law. They agree that he was a righteous prophet and caretaker at the sanctuary, and that the lots selected him when others also sought custody. His guardianship gave Maryam access to his knowledge and righteous conduct.

### In short

- Allah accepted Maryam’s dedication and gave her a good upbringing.
- Zakariyyā became her guardian after the caretakers settled their dispute by lots.
- Maryam received food out of season and recognized Allah as its provider.

38.text:
After seeing Allah provide Maryam with food out of season, “Then and there Zachariah prayed to his Lord” (3:38). He asks for a righteous child despite his old age and his wife’s barrenness. The provision he witnessed makes him hopeful that Allah can grant what is normally beyond reach. He turns to Allah, who hears every supplication.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Then and there Zachariah prayed to his Lord”** connects Zakariyyā’s prayer to what he had just seen in Maryam’s sanctuary. She had received summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer. One explanation says that witnessing this unusual provision strengthened his hope that Allah could also give him a child in old age. Zakariyyā had no child at that time, and he and his wife were elderly. He nevertheless believed in Allah’s power and prayed.

**“My Lord! Grant me—by your grace—righteous offspring”** is a request for a good child, not for wealth or worldly status. An inward explanation says that Zakariyyā sought a child to help him obey Allah and continue the work of prophethood, upholding the ḥaqq, the right due to Allah. The request was directed to Allah’s cause rather than the desires of the nafs, the lower self. He knew that a child at his age would be outside the ordinary course of events, but he asked Allah for His favor.

The Qur’an mentions that messengers before Muhammad ﷺ had wives and children (13:38). Another prayer asks for spouses and children who will be a comfort to the eyes because they obey Allah (25:74). Together these passages show that asking for righteous children is a good prayer. The explanation also says that marriage and family life are part of the Sunnah of the Messenger, and that a person who is able to marry and fulfill a spouse’s rights should not turn away from marriage. One report gives the Prophet’s encouragement to marry loving, fertile women so that the community may grow.

A report about Umm Sulaym illustrates prayer for children and blessing. She asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for her attendant Anas. He prayed that Allah increase Anas’s wealth and children and bless what he had been given. Anas later had about a hundred children and abundant wealth, according to the account.

**“You are certainly the Hearer of ˹all˺ prayers”** expresses Zakariyyā’s trust that Allah hears those who call upon Him. His prayer is made with humility, and he knows that Allah is able to answer it in a way no human could arrange.

### Why did Zakariyyā ask after seeing Maryam’s provision?

The fruit in the miḥrāb, the sanctuary where Maryam worshipped, was a sign that Allah provides beyond ordinary seasons. Zakariyyā saw that provision and became hopeful. His prayer does not imply that he doubted Allah’s power. Rather, the sign moved him to ask for a blessing that he had not thought possible under the usual conditions of age and barrenness.

### In short

- Zakariyyā prayed after seeing Allah provide Maryam with food out of season.
- He asked for righteous offspring to help in worship and the work of faith.
- Allah hears supplication and can answer beyond ordinary expectations.

39.text:
While Zakariyyā stood in prayer in the miḥrāb, “the angels called out to him” (3:39) with the news that Allah would grant him Yaḥyā (John). The child would confirm the word of Allah, become a noble and chaste leader, and be a prophet among the righteous. This is the answer to Zakariyyā’s supplication.

### Phrase by phrase

**“So the angels called out to him while he stood praying in the sanctuary”** places the good news during Zakariyyā’s worship. One explanation identifies the angel as Gabriel. The miḥrāb is the sanctuary or place of prayer. An inward reading says that a person who remains at the door of a king’s court continues to ask until the request is granted. It compares this to staying devoted in service to Allah rather than turning away from Him.

**“Allah gives you good news of ˹the birth of˺ John”** promises Zakariyyā a son named Yaḥyā. One explanation connects his name with life because Allah fills his heart with faith. Another says that the news revives his mother, who had been barren, and gives spiritual life to believers. Zakariyyā had asked for a child, and the angels now answer his supplication.

**“who will confirm the Word of Allah”** refers to ʿĪsā (Jesus), son of Maryam. He is called a word from Allah because he was created by Allah’s command without a father. Yaḥyā would affirm the truth of ʿĪsā’s message. The same description of Allah’s power appears in the account of Mūsā (Moses), whose mother was told that Allah would return him to her and make him a messenger (28:7).

**“and will be a great leader”** translates the quality sayyid. The explanations describe Yaḥyā as noble, wise, learned, pious, and honored by Allah. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Thawrī, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk explain the word through nobility, wisdom, and piety. Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib describes a sayyid as a scholar and jurist. ʿAṭiyyah emphasizes noble conduct and piety. ʿIkrimah says he was not overcome by anger. Ibn Zayd calls him noble, while Mujāhid says he was honored by Allah. These explanations present leadership as character and service, not merely authority.

**“chaste”** describes Yaḥyā’s protection from unlawful sexual conduct and domination by desire. One explanation says this does not necessarily mean he never married. Zakariyyā had asked for offspring, so the description can mean that Yaḥyā was protected from unlawful relations while remaining able to have a family lawfully. Another explanation describes him as abstinent from women and other ordinary pleasures because he was wholly occupied with worship. A further inward reading says he was free from bondage to created things and had realized ʿubūdiyya, true servanthood to Allah. These are explanations of his exceptional devotion, not a general rejection of lawful family life.

**“and a prophet among the righteous”** promises more than the birth of a son. Yaḥyā would himself receive prophethood and join the righteous. The good news includes his mission, not only his arrival. Some explanations also say that his mother’s barrenness would be overcome, just as the mother of Mūsā received good news about her son’s future mission (28:7).

Among those named in the explanations of Yaḥyā’s qualities are al-Baṣrī, Qatādah, Abū Ash-Shaʿthāʾ, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ bin Anas, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib, ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Zayd, and Mujāhid. Their comments explain the promise as a child of faith, noble leadership, chastity, and prophethood.

### What does “chaste” mean here?

The explanations distinguish protection from unlawful desire from a universal rule against marriage. Some understand Yaḥyā’s quality as complete abstinence, while another clarifies that it does not mean he could not marry lawfully. The descriptions agree that he was protected from wrongdoing and devoted to Allah.

### In short

- The angels announced Yaḥyā’s birth while Zakariyyā was praying.
- Yaḥyā would confirm ʿĪsā, the word created by Allah’s command.
- He would be a noble, chaste, and righteous prophet.

40.text:
Zachariah (Zakariyyā) asks how he can have a son when he is very old and his wife is barren. The answer is that “Allah does what He wills” (3:40). His question seeks to understand how the promise will happen, not to deny Allah’s power. Zachariah asks about its timing and circumstances, while the Qur’anic explanation affirms that Allah’s will is sufficient. Atiyah’s explanation of the promised child’s title sayyid emphasizes noble conduct, a quality that follows from this same promise.

### Phrase by phrase

**“My Lord!”** Zakariyyā’s question expresses amazement at the news, not rejection of it. He and his wife were both advanced in age, and she had been unable to bear children. One account gives Zakariyyā’s age as 120 and his wife’s as 98. Their circumstances make the promised birth extraordinary.

The question is not a rejection of the angels’ message. Zakariyyā already believes that Allah can create and provide beyond ordinary causes. He asks about the manner of the birth: will their condition change, or will a child come while they remain as they are? One explanation says they would remain in their condition and Allah would grant them a child. Another says the question arose from eagerness to understand how the promise would be fulfilled. An allusive explanation offers several possibilities, including whether the child would be born through his wife or by another means, then affirms that the promise concerned a child from both of them. The answer came through Gabriel, who had brought the good news, and the Qur’an presents this birth as part of Allah’s path of prophethood. The announcement of Yahya’s qualities includes nobility and piety, which ʿAṭiyyah uses to explain the title sayyid.

The story recalls the miraculous birth of ʿĪsā (Jesus), son of Maryam, and the promise given to the mother of Mūsā (Moses). The creation of Yaḥyā is within Allah’s power even when it departs from ordinary expectation. The sign that will follow makes the pregnancy known to Zakariyyā (19:10), and the promise of a child through an unlikely circumstance recalls the good news given to Mūsā’s mother (28:7).

**“He replied, ‘So will it be. Allah does what He wills.’”** answers that Allah’s will is not limited by age or barrenness. Nothing escapes His power and nothing is beyond His ability. The reply does not say that the ordinary laws of nature have power over Allah. It says that Allah creates as He chooses and in His wisdom.

### Why did Zakariyyā ask how it could happen?

He had received good news that challenged ordinary experience. His question seeks clarity about the circumstances, not reassurance that Allah has power. He had already seen Allah provide Maryam with food outside its season. That sign had opened his heart to asking for a child, and now he learns that Allah will answer his prayer despite the age of both parents.

### In short

- Zakariyyā and his wife were elderly, and she was barren.
- His question expressed wonder about how the promise would occur, not doubt in Allah.
- Allah’s will is not restricted by ordinary causes.

41.text:
Zakariyyā asks Allah for a sign. He is told that he “will not ˹be able to˺ speak to people for three days except through gestures” (3:41). He can still remember Allah and glorify Him morning and evening. The sign directs him to gratitude and remembrance while the promise unfolds.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Zachariah said, ‘My Lord! Grant me a sign’”** means he asks for an indication that his wife is pregnant. One explanation says that he wants to rejoice and begin thanking Allah before the child is born. He is not asking because he doubts the promise. He wants a sign that will help him remain grateful.

**“Your sign is that you will not ˹be able to˺ speak to people for three days except through gestures”** describes a temporary inability to speak to people, not a lasting disability. Zakariyyā can communicate through signs. The period is also described as three nights (19:10). One explanation stresses that he was not mute because of bodily defect. Another says the sign was suited to his request because it turned him away from ordinary conversation and toward remembrance of Allah.

The verse also establishes that when a valid reason prevents speech, gestures can serve as communication. Al-Qurṭubī cites a report about the Prophet ﷺ asking a servant woman where Allah is. She pointed toward the sky, and he accepted her faith. The gesture conveyed what she intended to say. Zakariyyā’s supplication continues in another form through the remembrance and glorification he is commanded to perform.

**“Remember your Lord often”** commands Zakariyyā to keep Allah present in his heart and on his tongue. An inward explanation describes three levels of remembrance: praising and supplicating with the tongue, remembering inwardly in the heart, and recognizing Allah’s remembrance of the servant. It points to remembrance in battle (8:45), strong remembrance (2:200), and remembering Allah when one forgets (18:24).

**“and glorify ˹Him˺ morning and evening”** directs him to praise Allah at the beginning and end of the day. The sign is therefore not merely silence. It becomes an opportunity for prayer, thanks, and worship.

### Why was silence given as the sign?

Zakariyyā asked for a sign so that he could rejoice and give thanks in advance. The sign makes ordinary speech unavailable for a short time, while leaving him able to signal to people and remember Allah. One allusive explanation presents the silence as a special conversation with Allah: his tongue is restrained from people, while his attention turns more fully to the One who answered his prayer.

### In short

- Zakariyyā asks for a sign of his wife’s pregnancy.
- He cannot speak to people for three days but can communicate by gestures.
- He is commanded to remember and glorify Allah often, morning and evening.

42.text:
The angels tell Maryam, “Surely Allah has selected you, purified you, and chosen you over all women of the world” (3:42). Her selection reflects her devotion and purity, and her unique place among the women of her time. The verse honors her before describing the worship commanded in the next verse.

### Phrase by phrase

**“And ˹remember˺ when the angels said”** introduces the message given to Maryam by Allah’s command. One explanation says that Gabriel conveyed the message. Maryam is being prepared for a special test and for the birth of ʿĪsā (Jesus), without a father.

**“O Mary!”** addresses Maryam directly and recognizes her as the recipient of this honor. The words call her to understand her standing before Allah.

**“Surely Allah has selected you”** means Allah singled her out through worship, modesty, honor, and conviction. One report says that ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib heard the Prophet ﷺ describe Maryam, daughter of ʿImrān, as the best woman of her time, and Khadījah, daughter of Khuwaylid, as the best woman of the Prophet’s time. At-Tirmidhi recorded it, and it is also found in the Two Sahihs.

**“purified you”** means that Allah made her free of disbelief, indecency, and sin. One explanation adds that she was kept from harm. Another describes her as protected from physical contact with men. An inward reading says her purity included a beautiful protection from sin and a special immunity.
