The Qur’an says that every messenger was told that there is no deity except Allah and that He alone should be worshipped (21:25). It also says that a messenger was sent to every community to call them to worship Allah and avoid false gods (16:36). This is the foundation of tawḥīd, the oneness of Allah.

**“associate none with Him”** rules out worshipping an idol, a cross, fire, a false deity, or any created thing. It also rules out treating a human being as a partner in Allah’s right to be worshipped. The invitation is clear and direct: worship Allah alone.

**“nor take one another as lords instead of Allah”** means that people must not obey religious leaders or rulers when they command disobedience to Allah. Ibn Jurayj explains that the prohibition is against obeying one another in disobedience to Allah. It does not forbid ordinary cooperation or respect. It rejects giving a human being the authority to make disobedience into a religion.

An inward reading applies the same warning to the self. The heart should not obey its commanding desires or treat blameworthy caprice as a lord. A person seeking truth should keep to one concern, rather than letting scattered attachments control the heart. The reading connects this to the promise of being in a seat of truthfulness in the Hereafter (54:55), and to the command not to take two gods (16:51).

**“But if they turn away”** means that the People of the Book may refuse the invitation. Their refusal does not require the Prophet to abandon his own belief or continue disputing without end.

**“then say, ‘Bear witness that we have submitted ˹to Allah alone˺’”** tells the Prophet to restate the Muslims’ position. If the other side rejects a clear common principle, the Muslims should bear witness to their submission to Allah and conclude the exchange. This keeps the ummah on the path of tawḥīd without endless quarrels.

### How should a message to another community begin?

One explanation draws a principle for preaching and dialogue from the verse. When speaking to people whose beliefs differ, begin with a truth both sides can recognize, such as the oneness of Allah. The Prophet’s letter to Heraclius, leader of the Romans, called him to Islam and promised safety and a double reward if he accepted. It warned that if he turned away, he would bear responsibility for his subjects. The letter then used the invitation to worship Allah alone. Al-Bukhārī records the letter.

The verse also has a connection to the delegation from Najrān. Muhammad bin Ishaq and Az-Zuhrī differ in how they relate the delegation’s agreement to pay. The opening of Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān and many verses after it are linked to this delegation. The people of Najrān came to al-Madīnah before al-Ḥudaybiyyah and before the conquest of Makkah, and before the later ruling on jizyah (9:29). One account says their payment was part of a settlement in place of mubāhalah, not the later jizyah tax. The verse prescribing jizyah came afterward and supported the arrangement already made with them.

An earlier event also shows that a practice may precede the verse that later confirms a ruling. ʿAbd Allāh bin Jaḥsh divided booty during an expedition before Badr, and a later revelation established the rule of one-fifth for the Prophet and four-fifths for the fighters. The Qur’an also came in agreement with things ʿUmar had said, including taking the Station of Ibrāhīm as a place of prayer (2:125), the hijab, the treatment of captives at Badr, and not praying for hypocrites. One other statement concerned the possibility that the Prophet’s wives could be replaced by better wives (66:5). These examples show that revelation may affirm a sound judgment already made.

### In short

- The common term is worshipping Allah alone and associating no partners with Him.
- No person should be obeyed as a lord when that obedience means disobeying Allah.
- If the People of the Book turn away, Muslims should affirm their submission and end the dispute.

65.text:
The verse challenges the People of the Book: “Why do you argue about Abraham” (3:65), when the Torah and Gospel came long after him? The Jews and Christians cannot claim that Ibrāhīm (Abraham) belonged to a religious community that arose after his time.

### Phrase by phrase

**“O People of the Book!”** again addresses Jews and Christians, here in response to their claims about Ibrāhīm, also called al-Khalīl, the intimate friend of Allah.

**“Why do you argue about Abraham”** refers to their dispute over whether he was a Jew or a Christian. The Jews claimed him as one of their own, and the Christians made the corresponding claim for their religion. Some would say that their traditions preserved the claim, but the Torah and Gospel came after Ibrāhīm. Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Jewish rabbis and Christian leaders argued this in front of the Prophet ﷺ. The verse rejects the claim from both sides.

**“while the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until long after him?”** means that Ibrāhīm lived before the revelation of the Torah to Mūsā (Moses) and before the Gospel given to ʿĪsā (Jesus). Judaism and Christianity, in the forms being debated, came later. Ibrāhīm could not have followed a scripture or community that had not yet appeared.

**“Do you not understand”** calls them to use reason. They argue from religious identities that arose after Ibrāhīm, even though their own scriptures show the order of events. Their claim is not supported by chronology.

The question does not forbid debate on matters people know. It rebukes disputing about a time and person concerning which they have no knowledge. It would be better to discuss the law they actually received than to invent a connection to Ibrāhīm.

### What is the proper limit of religious argument?

A person should not make confident claims about what they do not know. The People of the Book have knowledge of their own later revelations, but they cannot use them to rewrite the history of Ibrāhīm. Allah knows what they do not. The verse exposes the error of arguing from inherited labels rather than evidence.

An inward reading describes possessiveness as a cloak and jealousy as a veil over the heart. These veils cut people off from the truth about Ibrāhīm and make them cling to claims that do not fit the historical sequence. The word ḥijāb, a veil, here describes how pride can block understanding.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm lived before the Torah and Gospel were revealed.
- Jews and Christians cannot claim he belonged to communities that arose later.
- Religious argument must stay within what people can actually know.

66.text:
The verse distinguishes between informed discussion and baseless claims: “Allah knows and you do not know” (3:66). The People of the Book have some knowledge of their own scriptures, but they argue about Ibrāhīm’s time and religion without evidence. Allah alone knows the full reality.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Here you are! You disputed about what you have ˹little˺ knowledge of”** refers to matters the Jews and Christians know from their own scriptures, including the accounts of Mūsā and ʿĪsā. Their knowledge is limited, but at least they have a text to discuss.

**“but why do you now argue about what you have no knowledge of?”** rebukes their claims about Ibrāhīm. Their books do not establish that he was Jewish or Christian. They argue without proof about a period before those communities existed.

**“Allah knows”** means that Allah knows Ibrāhīm’s actual belief, the truth of his history, and what people later claimed about him. He knows the seen and unseen and the reality of every matter.

**“and you do not know”** reminds the disputants that human knowledge is limited. They should refer what they do not know to Allah rather than make unsupported claims. One inward reading says that a person should not judge matters for which there is no decisive proof or way of knowing.

The verse criticizes not only an incorrect conclusion but the habit of speaking beyond one’s knowledge. A person can know something about the Torah or Gospel and still know nothing about a period that preceded them. To say that Abraham followed a later religion goes beyond what those writings establish. Knowledge of one subject does not grant authority over every other subject.

### In short

- The People of the Book know something about their scriptures but lack evidence for their claims about Ibrāhīm.
- Allah knows the truth of his religion and history.
- People should not argue confidently about matters they do not know.

67.text:
The verse gives the answer: “Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian” (3:67). He submitted to Allah in uprightness and was not a polytheist. His religion was tawḥīd before the later labels arose.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian”** rejects both claims made about him. Ibrāhīm lived before the Torah and Gospel, so he belonged to neither later religious community.

**“he submitted in all uprightness”** describes him as a Muslim, one who submits to Allah. The word ḥanīf means turning away from false religions toward the upright path of worshipping Allah alone. It does not mean following a crooked path or constantly shifting according to personal advantage.

One inward explanation connects ḥanīf with mustaqīm, standing straight in truth. It pictures Ibrāhīm as unwavering in his submission, ready to surrender his wealth, himself, and even his son to Allah’s decree. His uprightness was not a label but a complete state of trust and obedience.

**“and was not a polytheist”** means he did not associate partners with Allah. He rejected shirk and lived with iman, faith in Allah alone. The Makkan idolaters later claimed the religion of Ibrāhīm for themselves, but his way was the opposite of worshipping idols or assigning divine power to created things.

The verse also warns that people in every age can use the names of prophets and saints to defend later additions to religion. Over time, people may mistake those changes for the original teaching. When someone calls them back to pure monotheism, opponents may accuse that person of rejecting the religion of their ancestors. The claim of connection to Ibrāhīm is not enough. The true measure is following his tawḥīd and submission.

The Qur’an makes the same point in al-Baqarah: the claim that people must become Jews or Christians in order to be guided is rejected (2:135). Ibrāhīm’s faith precedes those identities and points to the worship of Allah alone.

### What does it mean to be a ḥanīf?

A ḥanīf turns away from idolatry and false belief toward worship of Allah alone. Ibrāhīm’s uprightness included steadfast faith, surrender, and refusal to trade truth for personal gain. He was neither Jew nor Christian, but a servant devoted to Allah.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm was not part of religions that arose after him.
- He was a Muslim and ḥanīf, upright in the worship of Allah alone.
- He rejected shirk and submitted fully to Allah.

68.text:
The verse identifies those with the closest claim to Ibrāhīm: “those who have the best claim to Abraham are his followers, this Prophet, and the believers” (3:68). A true connection is shown by following his religion of tawḥīd, not by merely claiming his name. Allah is the Protector of the believers.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Indeed, those who have the best claim to Abraham”** means those most entitled to say that they follow his way. The Jewish and Christian leaders claimed that Ibrāhīm belonged to them, but their religious forms came later. The stronger claim belongs to the people who follow his actual faith.

**“are his followers”** first includes those who followed Ibrāhīm during his own time and adhered to his worship of Allah alone. A person’s closeness to a prophet is measured by faith and obedience, not by ancestry or a later label.

**“this Prophet”** refers to Muhammad ﷺ. His message agrees with Ibrāhīm’s tawḥīd and restores the call to worship Allah alone. He has a stronger claim to Ibrāhīm than those who reject his message while claiming to follow Ibrāhīm.

**“and the believers”** refers to the Prophet’s community and those who follow its guidance. This includes the Muhājirūn, the Anṣār, and those who follow their example. The believers accept Ibrāhīm, Mūsā, ʿĪsā, and all Allah’s messengers without dividing them into rival groups.

Saʿīd bin Manṣūr records a report from Ibn Masʿūd that every prophet had a walī, a close supporter, from among the prophets. The Prophet ﷺ said that his walī among them was his father Ibrāhīm, the khalīl, intimate friend, of his Lord. This describes a spiritual bond through the shared message of tawḥīd.

Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that Jewish leaders told Muhammad ﷺ that they had a better claim to Ibrāhīm’s religion and accused him of envy. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ghanm is also named among those who transmitted this account. The verse answers that claim by defining closeness through following Ibrāhīm’s religion, not through an assertion of superiority. The people of al-ḥaqq, the people of truth, are those who hold to this religion of tawḥīd.

A historical report then describes the wider struggle around the early Muslim community. Jaʿfar bin Abī Ṭālib and his companions migrated to Abyssinia. Muhammad ﷺ migrated to al-Madīnah, and the Battle of Badr followed. After losing people at Badr, Quraysh gathered at Dār al-Nadwah and planned to seek the return of the Muslim emigrants from the Negus. ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ and ʿUmārah bin Abī Muʿayṭ were sent with gifts and tanned skins to Abyssinia. They tried to persuade the Negus that the emigrants followed a liar and should be returned. This account shows how the community’s claim to Ibrāhīm was tested by migration, persecution, and steadfastness.

**“And Allah is the Guardian of those who believe”** means that Allah is their walī, their Protector, Helper, and Preserver. The believers are entrusted with His religion and hold to the declaration of His oneness. Allah’s friendship brings aid, selection, nearness, and protection. The claim to Ibrāhīm is therefore joined to Allah’s care for those who follow the truth.

### Who has the strongest claim to Ibrāhīm?

The strongest claim belongs to those who follow Ibrāhīm’s religion of submission and tawḥīd. This includes Muhammad ﷺ and the believers who accept all Allah’s messengers. A name or inherited identity cannot replace faith and obedience.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm’s true followers, Muhammad ﷺ, and the believers have the best claim to him.
- The believers’ connection is through tawḥīd and following the messengers.
- Allah is their Protector, Helper, and Guardian.

69.text:
The verse warns believers: “Some of the People of the Book wish to mislead you” (3:69). Their effort will not take the believers away from the truth. Instead, the harm of their attempt returns upon themselves, though they do not understand what they are doing.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Some of the People of the Book”** refers to a group among the Jews and Christians, not every individual. The verse describes people who oppose the new Muslim community and want its members to abandon their faith.

**“wish to mislead you ˹believers˺”** means they hope to turn Muslims away from Islam. One report connects the verse to Kaʿb al-Ashraf after the Battle of Uḥud. He invited three companions, Muʿādh, Ḥudhayfah al-Yamān, and ʿAmmār bin Yāsir, to leave Islam and adopt Judaism. They did not accept the invitation.

The invitation tries to use the authority of an older religious community to unsettle new believers. The People of the Book had received the Torah and Injīl, but that did not give them permission to hide the truth or demand that Muslims follow their religion. A person should judge a claim by its truth, not by the age or reputation of the group presenting it.

**“They mislead none but themselves”** means their attempt does not overturn the believers’ faith. The plot only adds to the plotters’ own error and accountability. They may hope to make others follow them, but their actions deepen their own misguidance.

**“yet they fail to perceive it”** means they do not recognize the outcome of their conduct. They think they are weakening the believers, but they are exposing their own rejection of truth. The verse gives the believers confidence that deceptive efforts cannot defeat Allah’s guidance.

### Why does their attempt mislead only themselves?

Their strategy is rooted in envy and in the wish to keep others from accepting Muhammad ﷺ. The following verses 70 and 71 explain that they reject signs they recognize and conceal truth they know. Their effort can expose their own wrongdoing, but it cannot cancel the guidance Allah has given the believers.

### In short

- Some among the People of the Book try to turn believers away from Islam.
- Their effort does not mislead the believers who hold to the truth.
- Their own rejection and deception increase their misguidance.

70.text:
The verse asks, “Why do you reject the signs of Allah while you bear witness” (3:70). The People of the Book recognize signs of the Prophet’s truth in their scriptures, yet still reject them. Their knowledge makes the rejection more serious.

### Phrase by phrase

**“O People of the Book!”** addresses Jews and Christians who have received earlier revelation. The statement concerns those who know what their own scriptures say about Allah’s messengers.

**“Why do you reject the signs of Allah”** means that they deny the verses and evidence Allah has given. The signs include descriptions of Muhammad ﷺ in the Torah and Injīl. One explanation says they know that these descriptions are true, yet refuse to accept the prophethood they indicate.

**“while you bear witness ˹to their truth˺”** means they acknowledge the signs or know the truth from their scriptures. They cannot reasonably claim that they have no evidence. Their testimony stands against their rejection.

One explanation stresses that disbelief, kufr, is intrinsically wrong and prohibited in every condition. The reference to knowledge and witness intensifies the rebuke. It does not mean disbelief would become permissible if a person lacked knowledge or did not openly testify.

The message also warns against treating revelation as a possession of one community. Recognition of a prophet’s signs creates a responsibility to follow the truth. It is not enough to preserve a scripture while refusing the messenger whose coming it describes.

### In short

- The People of the Book are challenged for rejecting Allah’s signs.
- They know that their scriptures contain evidence for Muhammad’s prophethood.
- Knowledge makes their deliberate rejection more blameworthy.

71.text:
The verse asks, “Why do you mix the truth with falsehood and hide the truth knowingly” (3:71). Some among the People of the Book distort what their scriptures say and conceal the descriptions of Muhammad ﷺ, despite knowing what they are hiding.

### Phrase by phrase

**“O People of the Book!”** again addresses those who have received revelation and should recognize the signs of a true messenger.

**“Why do you mix the truth with falsehood”** means they confuse genuine statements about the Prophet with invented claims or misleading interpretations. One explanation says they distort the descriptions of Muhammad ﷺ so that people will not recognize him. The mixture makes falsehood appear to have religious authority.

**“and hide the truth knowingly”** means they conceal what they know about his prophethood. The concealment is deliberate, not an innocent misunderstanding. Another explanation says some people publicly agree with Muslims to avoid trouble while privately remaining loyal to their own false claims.

The verse condemns both distortion and silence. A person may mislead by openly changing a statement, or by withholding the truth while allowing others to be deceived. In either case, knowledge brings responsibility.

### In short

- Some People of the Book mix true revelation with false interpretation.
- They conceal signs of Muhammad’s prophethood even though they know them.
- Deliberate concealment is not the same as honest uncertainty.

72.text:
The verse exposes a strategy of deception: “A group among the People of the Book said ˹to one another˺, ‘Believe in what has been revealed to the believers in the morning and reject it in the evening’” (3:72). They hope that a public change of position will make Muslims doubt their faith.

### Phrase by phrase

**“A group among the People of the Book said ˹to one another˺”** describes a plan discussed privately by some Jewish leaders. The verse does not accuse every person among them. It identifies a particular group that wants to manipulate how Muslims judge the new revelation.

**“Believe in what has been revealed to the believers in the morning”** means they would pretend to accept the Qur’an at the beginning of the day. One interpretation says twelve rabbis from Khaybar and Uraynah were to make the display. They would claim to have examined their scriptures and found Muhammad ﷺ genuine, so that Muslims would consider their apparent conversion powerful evidence.

Another interpretation connects the plan with the change of qiblah. The group would pray toward the Kaʿbah at the opening of the day, then reject it and return to Jerusalem at the end of the day. Their change would be presented as proof that they had discovered a flaw in the new religion. The Kaʿbah is connected with Abraham, and the change from Jerusalem was meant to provoke doubt. Kaʿb al-Ashraf is named among the leaders behind this plot. Mujāhid, Muqātil, and al-Kalbī connect the scheme to the qiblah change. Al-Suddī and al-Ḥasan mention the plan of the rabbis to feign belief and then reject it. They say the display should fool ordinary Muslims into thinking the learned had found a defect.

**“and reject it in the evening”** means that the group would reverse its public position. In the first interpretation, they pretended to believe and then announced disbelief. In the second, they followed one qiblah in the morning and another later. Either way, their aim was to make the believers think that learned people had found a reason to leave Islam.

**“so they may abandon their faith”** describes the intended result. The group hopes that Muslims will reason that people who know scripture better must have seen a defect in Islam. The plan depends on believers being impressed by an apparent religious expert rather than examining the claim itself.

This strategy fails because Allah reveals it to the Prophet and the believers. Its exposure prevents it from producing the confusion its planners expect. It also shows that a display of belief is not proof of sincerity if it is followed by a deliberate return to disbelief for the purpose of deception.

### Why use belief in the morning and rejection in the evening?

The quick reversal is meant to create doubt. The group thinks its religious learning will make Muslims trust the performance and assume the Qur’an has a defect. The verse explains the deception so that believers will not mistake a staged change of heart for evidence against their faith.

### In short

- A group plans to pretend to accept the revelation and then publicly reject it.
- Another interpretation connects the plan to switching the qiblah from the Kaʿbah back to Jerusalem.
- The aim is to make Muslims doubt, but Allah exposes the scheme.

73.text:
The plotters also say that only those who follow their religion should be trusted. The Prophet is told to answer: “Surely, ˹the only˺ true guidance is Allah’s guidance” (3:73). Guidance and all bounty belong to Allah, who gives them to whomever He wills.

### Phrase by phrase

**“And only believe those who follow your religion”** reports their instruction to keep their knowledge within their own religious group. They do not want Muslims to learn what they know from earlier scripture or use it as evidence. They fear that if others receive similar revelation, they will be able to argue against them before Allah.

The statement reflects envy and communal pride. They assume that guidance belongs only to their group and that Allah will not give it to anyone else. Another explanation says they try to keep Muslims from learning the descriptions of Muhammad ﷺ because those descriptions could be used to establish his prophethood.

**“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Surely, ˹the only˺ true guidance is Allah’s guidance’”** commands the Prophet to state that guidance is not controlled by a community. Allah gives it as He wills. The Jews’ refusal to acknowledge a messenger does not make their religion the standard of truth. The earlier qiblah had been toward Jerusalem, but Allah directed the Muslim community toward the Kaʿbah associated with Ibrāhīm. This change was part of His guidance, not a reason to return to an earlier direction.

The verse also answers those who fear that others might be given the same scripture, wisdom, or virtue. Allah’s guidance is not a limited possession that one group can guard against others. The Muslim ummah is favored with the Qur’an and the message of Muhammad ﷺ, while earlier communities received their own revelations. The law and religious paths of earlier communities were superseded by the final Sharīʿah. The Tariqah and deeper spiritual realities are also gifts from Allah, not privileges a group can demand.

The Qur’an describes the completion of the religion as a blessing (5:3). An inward reading says the Muslim community was given a final scripture, a final prophet, Ramadan, and Friday, and that earlier laws were superseded by the final law. It calls believers to gratitude and warns them not to lean toward wrongdoing (11:113).

**“Do not believe that someone will receive ˹revealed˺ knowledge similar to yours”** conveys their fear that Allah might favor another people with revelation and knowledge. They assume that the gifts they received must remain exclusive to them. The verse rejects that assumption.

**“or argue against you before your Lord”** means they fear that knowledge will become evidence against them on the Day of Judgment. If Muslims receive clear guidance, they can challenge claims that contradict it. The correct response to this possibility is not to hide revelation, but to accept the truth.

**“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Indeed, all bounty is in the Hands of Allah’”** means every gift, including prophethood, revelation, knowledge, and faith, comes from Allah. No community owns His favor.

**“He grants it to whoever He wills”** means Allah chooses those who are fit to receive His gifts. He grants knowledge and sound understanding to some and may leave others in misguidance when they turn away. His choice is based on wisdom, not on the claims people make about their ancestry.

**“And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing”** means Allah’s gifts are vast, and He knows who deserves them. He is not limited in what He can give and does not need permission from any community to grant revelation.

### Why does guidance not belong to one community?

The claim that only one group can receive revelation treats Allah’s bounty as if it were private property. The verse corrects that assumption. Allah’s guidance is given by His wisdom, and a community should respond to revelation with gratitude rather than envy or concealment.

### In short

- Guidance belongs to Allah, not to a single religious community.
- The People of the Book fear that others may receive knowledge and use it as evidence.
- Allah gives bounty, faith, and revelation to whomever He wills, with full knowledge.

74.text:
The verse concludes, “He chooses whoever He wills to receive His mercy” (3:74). Allah selects whom He wills for guidance and other blessings. His bounty is vast, and no one can claim that Allah’s mercy belongs only to their group.

### Phrase by phrase

**“He chooses whoever He wills”** means Allah selects whom He wills for His gifts. He may grant some people provision, others excellent character, worship, or spiritual insight. He chooses those who receive revelation and guidance according to His wisdom.

**“to receive His mercy”** includes guidance, prophethood, faith, and the ability to recognize the truth. Allah’s mercy is not confined to a nation or lineage. A person’s efforts do not force Allah to grant a particular spiritual station. Even when people strive in worship, their final salvation depends on His mercy.

The Qur’an reminds people that if they tried to count Allah’s blessings, they could not number them (14:34). Another verse describes people who hope for Allah’s mercy and fear His punishment (17:57). Hope and fear keep a believer from despair and from becoming arrogant about their deeds.

A hadith says that no one enters Paradise by deeds alone. When the Prophet ﷺ was asked whether this applied even to him, he said that he too would need Allah’s mercy to encompass him. The report teaches that righteous actions matter, but they do not make a person independent of Allah’s grace.

**“And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty”** means His generosity has no limit. He can grant guidance, knowledge, faith, and nearness to whom He wills. The verse answers envy by showing that Allah’s gifts are not diminished when He grants them to another person.

One inward reading describes different forms of mercy: outward provision, good character, worship, spiritual desire, and insight into the heart. Allah does not specify one group as the only recipient, so people may hope for His favor while remaining humble and fearful of falling short.

### In short

- Allah chooses whom He wills for guidance and mercy.
- His gifts include provision, character, worship, faith, and spiritual insight.
- Believers hope for His mercy and do not rely on deeds alone.

75.text:
The verse distinguishes between individuals: “There are some among the People of the Book who, if entrusted with a stack of gold, will readily return it” (3:75). Others will not return even a single coin unless the owner keeps demanding it. Their excuse that Arabs are not protected by their rules is a lie against Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**“There are some among the People of the Book”** means the verse is not describing every Jew or Christian. It identifies different kinds of people among them, including some who are trustworthy and some who are not.

**“who, if entrusted with a stack of gold, will readily return it”** describes a person who faithfully returns a large trust. One report identifies ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions as an example. A man entrusted Ibn Salām with 1200 plates of gold, and he returned them. His conduct is praised even though the discussion distinguishes worldly trustworthiness from acceptance of faith.

Praising a good deed does not necessarily mean that the person has received salvation. A good action can earn a good reputation in this world and may reduce punishment, even if the person is a kāfir, a disbeliever who has not accepted faith. This verse shows that Islam can recognize a virtue in someone outside the Muslim community without treating every aspect of that person’s belief as correct.

**“Yet there are others who, if entrusted with a single coin, will not repay it unless you constantly demand it”** describes a different kind of person. A report identifies Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf as one who refused to return a dinar entrusted to him by a man from Quraysh. The owner had to remain with him and insist on receiving what was owed.

**“This is because they say, ‘We are not accountable for ˹exploiting˺ the Gentiles’”** reports the excuse some used to justify taking the property of Arabs. They claimed that their religion did not hold them accountable for cheating people outside their community. This is a false claim, not a permission Allah gave them.

**“And ˹so˺ they attribute lies to Allah knowingly”** means they invent a religious justification for dishonesty while knowing it is false. Allah does not allow a person to take property without right merely because the owner belongs to another community.

Abdur-Razzaq records an exchange in which a man asked Ibn ʿAbbās about taking chickens and sheep from non-Muslims under Muslim protection during a battle. The man said they believed there was no sin in taking the property. Ibn ʿAbbās answered that this was the same false claim the People of the Book made. If people pay the jizyah, their property remains protected. It may not be taken unless they willingly give it.

The verse also supports the right of a creditor to keep pursuing a borrower until the debt is repaid. Abū Ḥanīfah derived this ruling from the words about having to keep standing over a person to recover what is owed. The wording is about insisting on a rightful claim, not permission to harass someone who has already paid.

### What is the difference between praising a person and approving their faith?

A person outside Islam may possess a real virtue, such as returning a trust. Recognizing that virtue is not the same as declaring every belief correct or promising salvation. The verse praises honest conduct while warning against using religious difference as an excuse for theft. It rejects prejudice in both directions: neither should a good deed be denied simply because of the person, nor should a false religious claim make dishonesty acceptable.

### In short

- Some People of the Book are trustworthy, while others cheat and refuse to return property.
- The verse condemns the claim that Arabs or Gentiles may be exploited without sin.
- Jizyah does not make a person’s property available to others.

76.text:
The verse corrects the excuse: “Those who honour their trusts and shun evil—surely Allah loves those who are mindful ˹of Him˺” (3:76). A person is accountable for promises and trusts, and Allah loves those who keep them and avoid wrongdoing.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Absolutely!”** rejects the claim that people may cheat those outside their community. There is a duty to return what belongs to another person.

**“Those who honour their trusts”** means those who fulfil a covenant with Allah and keep agreements with other people. A pledge to Allah includes faith in Him and His messenger, Muhammad ﷺ. A trust between people includes returning property and fulfilling what was promised.

**“and shun evil”** means being mindful of Allah by avoiding betrayal and other prohibitions. A person should not treat a promise as optional when it becomes inconvenient. The Sharīʿah sent with Muhammad ﷺ requires both faith and trustworthy conduct.

**“surely Allah loves those who are mindful ˹of Him˺”** means Allah rewards those who keep their commitments and avoid sin. The muttaqīn, those mindful of Allah, fear violating a trust and act with obedience.

The verse says that a promise made by one person and a covenant binding both parties require honesty. This duty is reinforced by the Prophet’s Sunnah and the Sharīʿah. The next verse warns of the serious outcome for those who trade Allah’s covenant and their oaths for a small worldly gain.

### In short

- A trust and a pledge must be honoured.
- Taqwā includes avoiding betrayal and fulfilling what is owed to others.
- Allah loves the muttaqīn who keep their commitments.

77.text:
The verse warns of those “who trade Allah’s covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain” (3:77). They sacrifice their obligations for a small worldly benefit and will have no share in the Hereafter. Allah will not speak to them kindly, look upon them with mercy, or purify them, and they will face painful punishment.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Indeed, those who trade Allah’s covenant and their oaths”** means those who break what they have pledged to Allah and use oaths falsely to obtain another person’s property. The covenant includes accepting the truth and following the messenger whose description they know from the Torah and other scriptures. An oath is not a tool for turning a false claim into a right. The verse says that such a person has no lot, no share, in the Hereafter.

One explanation says the covenant is an agreement made between parties that both must honour. It differs from a promise made by only one side. Both have moral weight, but the verse especially condemns breaking solemn commitments and invoking Allah’s name to deceive.

**“for a fleeting gain”** means a small benefit in this short life, such as a piece of land, goods in a sale, or property obtained through a false oath. The gain may appear valuable to the one taking it, but it is temporary compared with what is lost in the Hereafter.

**“will have no share in the Hereafter”** means that they will receive none of the reward prepared for the righteous. They have chosen worldly advantage over their final outcome, ʿuqbāhum. Their oath may win a dispute in the eyes of people, but it cannot change what Allah knows.

**“Allah will neither speak to them”** means He will not address them with words of kindness or glad tidings on the Day of Judgment. This is a sign of His anger toward their dishonesty.

**“nor look at them”** means He will not look upon them with mercy. They will stand before Him without the favor they hoped their worldly gain would secure.

**“nor purify them on the Day of Judgment”** means He will not cleanse them of their sins or make them worthy of the Garden. One explanation says that violating the rights of another person is especially serious because Allah does not simply forgive what one person owes another without justice being done.

**“And they will suffer a painful punishment”** completes the warning. The five consequences are loss of the Hereafter’s reward, no kind speech from Allah, no merciful regard, no purification, and painful punishment.

### Hadith warnings about false oaths and broken trusts

A report from Abū Dharr says there are three kinds of people whom Allah will not speak to, look at with mercy, or purify on the Day of Resurrection, and who will suffer a painful punishment. They are a man whose garment hangs below his ankles, a person who swears falsely to sell merchandise, and someone who gives charity but reminds the recipient of it. Aḥmad recorded the report, and Muslim and the Sunan compilers also transmitted it.

Another report concerns a dispute over land between Imruʾ al-Qays bin ʿĀbis, a man from Kindah, and a man from Hadramut. The Prophet ﷺ asked the claimant from Ḥaḍramawt for evidence, but he had none. Imruʾ al-Qays was then asked to swear. The other man warned that, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah, a false oath would cost him his land. The Prophet said that whoever swears falsely to take another person’s property will meet Allah while Allah is angry with him. Imruʾ al-Qays asked what he would gain by giving up the dispute. The Prophet answered that he would gain Paradise, and Imruʾ al-Qays relinquished the land. An-Nasāʾī recorded this report.

A report from ʿAbd Allāh, known as Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, says that whoever takes a Muslim’s property through a false oath will meet Allah while He is angry with him. Al-Ashʿath said that the verse was revealed concerning his own dispute with a Jewish man over land. He complained to the Prophet ﷺ, who asked whether he had evidence. He did not. The other man was asked to swear, and al-Ashʿath feared that a false oath would make him lose his property. The Two Sahihs recorded the report.

Abū Hurayrah reports another warning about three kinds of people. One refuses a wayfarer some of the water he has. Another swears falsely after the afternoon prayer to complete a sale. The third gives allegiance to a Muslim ruler but only fulfils the pledge when given something in return. Abū Dāwūd and At-Tirmidhī recorded the report, and At-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

These reports say clearly that the verse is not limited to disputes between religious communities. The Prophet’s Sunnah also warns against these actions. False oaths, dishonest sales, withholding basic help, and conditional loyalty all violate obligations. The warning applies whenever a person uses Allah’s name to take what is not rightfully theirs.

### Why is a small gain called a trade?

The person exchanges a lasting share in the Hereafter for a temporary benefit. The exchange is deeply unequal. A piece of land or profit from a sale cannot compensate for losing Allah’s mercy and facing punishment. A truthful person may even give up an immediate advantage, as Imruʾ al-Qays did, to preserve a claim to the Garden.

### In short

- A false oath cannot make another person’s property lawful.
- Allah warns of five consequences for those who trade His covenant and their oaths for gain.
- Hadith reports apply the warning to dishonest sales, land disputes, charity, and broken pledges.

78.text:
The verse warns that “There are some among them who distort the Book with their tongues” (3:78). They make their own words seem to come from revelation, then knowingly attribute those lies to Allah. The warning includes both changing the wording and twisting its meaning.

### Phrase by phrase

**“There are some among them”** refers to a group among the People of the Book, not every person who follows an earlier scripture. One report identifies Kaʿb al-Ashraf and his companions among those who mislead people by distorting the text.

**“who distort the Book with their tongues”** means they alter words while reciting or explaining scripture. Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas explain this as changing Allah’s words. Another explanation says the distortion can be false interpretation, even when a person cannot remove the original words from Allah’s preserved revelation.

The Torah and Injīl are the earlier books discussed here. Wahb bin Munabbih says they remain as Allah revealed them, while people mislead others through additions, false interpretations, and books they wrote themselves. Another view notes that copies currently in human hands have also experienced additions and deletions. The distinction is between Allah’s original revelation, which He preserves, and the ways people may alter or misrepresent its text and meaning.

**“to make you think this ˹distortion˺ is from the Book”** describes the purpose of the deception. The speaker wants the listener to mistake an invented reading for revelation. This can confuse people who do not know the scripture well.

**“but it is not what the Book says”** exposes the false claim. A person’s words do not become scripture merely because they are read with a religious voice or attributed to a holy book.

**“They say, ‘It is from Allah’”** shows the seriousness of the lie. They attach divine authority to their own words.

**“but it is not from Allah”** denies that attribution. Allah did not reveal what they invented.

**“And ˹so˺ they attribute lies to Allah knowingly”** means they understand that they are misrepresenting revelation. Their speech is not an honest mistake but a deliberate falsehood.

An inward reading applies the warning to those who claim spiritual knowledge on the Ṭarīqa, the path of spiritual discipline, while their hearts have not verified what their tongues say. They embellish words to impress ordinary people and beginners. Religious language does not make a claim true if the speaker has no knowledge of it.

### Why is the distortion deliberate?

The verse says the group knows what it is doing. They want their own additions and readings to carry the authority of the Torah or Injīl. The warning applies equally to anyone on the Ṭarīqa who claims spiritual insight without knowledge or verification.

### In short

- Some people distort scripture through altered wording or false interpretation.
- The Torah and Injīl are not the same as later human claims made in their name.
- Knowingly attributing a lie to Allah is a serious offense.

79.text:
The verse says it is impossible for a prophet to ask people to worship him: “It is not appropriate for someone who Allah has blessed with the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood” (3:79). Such a person calls people to become devoted servants of the Lord, teaching and studying scripture.

### Phrase by phrase

**“It is not appropriate for someone”** means that no true messenger would contradict the very purpose of his mission by calling people to worship him. This was relevant when Christians from Najrān discussed ʿĪsā (Jesus), and some Muslims asked whether they should prostrate before Muhammad ﷺ instead of greeting him. They addressed the Prophet as Abū al-Qāsim. Neither prophet would ask for worship.

**“who Allah has blessed with the Scripture”** refers to a person given revelation. The scripture is a trust to convey, not a tool for gaining personal devotion.

**“wisdom”** includes understanding, sound judgment, and knowledge of the law, Al-Hukm. A prophet knows the difference between Allah’s command and human desire.

**“and prophethood”** means Allah has chosen him to deliver a message. Allah knows whom to select for this task (6:124). This selection rules out the idea that a prophet would turn people away from Allah toward himself.

**“to say to people, ‘Worship me instead of Allah’”** would be a direct call to kufr, disbelief. No prophet can instruct people to commit shirk by associating him with Allah. The messengers convey what Allah commands and forbid what He forbids.

**“Rather, he would say, ‘Be devoted to the worship of your Lord ˹alone˺’”** means the prophet calls people to become devoted to Allah. All messengers brought this same central teaching: worship Allah alone (16:36, 21:25). The Qur’an asks whether Allah appointed other gods to be worshipped (43:45). It also warns that an angel who claimed to be a god would be punished (21:29).

**“in accordance with what these prophets read in the Scripture and what they taught”** connects learning with practice. The word Rabbāniyyūn describes learned, wise people who teach the Book and study it. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk explain it as people who are wise, knowledgeable, and forbearing. Ibn ʿAbbās also says that Allah’s words cannot be removed from His books, even though people may distort their apparent meanings. Ibn Abī Ḥātim records Wahb bin Munabbih’s statement about additions and false interpretation. Knowledge should make people better servants of Allah, not servants of a human teacher.

One inward reading describes the Rabbāniyyūn as people singled out for Allah, with sincere intention, trust, and intimacy. It speaks of being characterized by Allah’s good qualities, while remaining a servant. Abū al-Qāsim Kurragānī says that the traveler remains on the path while acquiring these qualities and has not yet reached the destination. This spiritual description still rejects worship of any prophet or teacher.

The same reading describes the long remembrance of Allah as a sign of spiritual aspiration. It says that the seeker waits for the remembrance to bear fruit and seeks closeness to Allah rather than worldly power. The Prophet ﷺ is called Muṣṭafā, the chosen one, but his distinction does not make him an object of worship. True closeness means servanthood to Allah.

The verse also answers the claim that Ibrāhīm’s religion permitted people to worship human beings. Allah had already instructed Abraham and his descendants to submit to Him (2:132). No prophet, including Abraham, Adam, or Jesus, ever called people to worship him. The messenger’s task is to bring the ummah to Allah, not to make himself its god.

### What does it mean to be Rabbāniyyūn?

They are people who learn scripture, teach it, and put its guidance into practice. Their knowledge leads to faith and service. A true teacher directs people toward Allah, not toward the worship of the teacher.

### In short

- A prophet blessed with scripture and prophethood does not call people to worship him.
- Prophets call people to worship Allah alone and to become learned servants of their Lord.
- Spiritual insight and remembrance deepen servanthood but never make a human being divine.

80.text:
The verse continues: “And he would never ask you to take angels and prophets as lords” (3:80). No messenger would tell people to worship created beings or to reject Allah after submitting to Him.

### Phrase by phrase

**“And he would never ask you”** means a prophet would not issue a command that contradicts his message. The same applies to a true religious teacher: he does not make people’s worship a condition of following him.

**“to take angels and prophets as lords”** means treating them as objects of worship or as independent sources of divine power. Some Jews elevated ʿUzayr (Ezra), and some Christians elevated ʿĪsā. Some polytheists among Quraysh treated angels as daughters of Allah. The verse rejects these forms of shirk.

A prophet may be honored and obeyed as Allah’s messenger, but he is not worshipped. Allah instructed Abraham and his children to submit to Him (2:132). The Torah, Gospel, and Qur’an all direct people toward worshipping Allah alone. The verse says that no prophet asks people to replace Allah with another lord. The Sharīʿah commands respect for prophets while denying that any created being shares in al-rubūbiyya, the Lordship that belongs to the Real alone.

An inward reading says that no created thing has independent power to establish good or evil. It uses the word ithbāt for attributing existence or power to something. The believer may honor a messenger and follow his law, but must not give created forms the status of divine lordship. When the lights of tawḥīd appear in the heart, the person stops treating outward appearances as independent powers.

**“Would he ask you to disbelieve after you have submitted”** means that a messenger would not call people away from iman, faith, after they have surrendered to Allah. Submission and worship of created beings cannot coexist. If a claim asks someone to reject Allah’s oneness, that claim is not from a prophet.

One interpretation connects the phrase with the claim that Muhammad ﷺ asked people to love or worship him as Christians worship ʿĪsā. The verse rejects that claim. A messenger asks for obedience to Allah, not worship of himself.

### Why would a messenger never teach this?

A messenger’s mission is to call people to the worship of Allah and to the faith shared by Abraham and the prophets. If he demanded worship for himself or another created being, he would contradict the revelation and the submission he was sent to teach.

### In short

- Prophets and angels are honored servants, not lords to be worshipped.
- No messenger would command shirk or disbelief after submission to Allah.
- Tawḥīd affirms Allah’s lordship alone while allowing respect for His messengers.

81.text:
Allah recalls a covenant made with the prophets: “if there comes to you a messenger confirming what you have, you must believe in him and support him” (3:81). Every prophet was to accept a later messenger who confirmed Allah’s revelation and help him.

### Phrase by phrase

**“˹Remember˺ when Allah made a covenant with the prophets”** refers to a solemn pledge taken from the prophets Allah sent, from Adam through ʿĪsā. It concerns their duty to believe in and support a messenger who comes after them with confirmation of what Allah gave them.

**“Now that I have given you the Book and wisdom”** means Allah has already granted revelation and understanding. The prophets are not being asked to abandon their own missions. They are asked to recognize that Allah may send a later messenger who continues and confirms the same truth.

**“if there comes to you a messenger confirming what you have”** is understood by many as referring to Muhammad ﷺ, the final messenger, whose message confirms the earlier scriptures. The prophets were to accept and support him if he appeared in their lifetimes. One report also says the prophets were instructed to describe Muhammad’s qualities to their communities.

A further interpretation says the covenant required every prophet to believe in the messengers who came before and after him. These readings do not contradict one another: all prophets affirm the same revelation from Allah and support one another’s truth.

**“you must believe in him and support him”** means more than private recognition. The prophets were to affirm the messenger and assist his mission. The obligation includes their communities, who were to follow the covenant made through their prophets.

**“He added, ‘Do you affirm this covenant and accept this commitment?’”** asks the prophets to confirm their pledge and accept its binding force. They answer that they do. Allah then makes them witnesses to the covenant.

**“Then bear witness, and I too am a Witness”** means the prophets testify to the agreement, while Allah Himself witnesses it. The pledge is therefore known and binding. Turning away from it is not a minor mistake.

One report from ʿAbd Allāh bin ʿAbbās says Allah never sent a prophet without taking this pledge: if Muhammad ﷺ appeared during that prophet’s lifetime, he would believe in and support him. ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib and Ibn ʿAbbās are also named in this explanation. Qatādah and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī say that the prophets pledged to believe in one another. The report is described with a ḥasan grade.

This pledge follows the earlier covenant in which Allah called the children of Adam to witness that He is their Lord (7:172). The covenant is also connected to the Prophet’s night journey, when he led the prophets in prayer at Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem. The prophets’ gathering signifies their unity in the truth and Muhammad’s place as their leader. He is promised al-Maqām al-Maḥmūd, the praised station of intercession (17:79), which the other prophets will leave for him on the Day of Gathering.

Gabriel and Michael are included in the allusive explanation of the covenant. It describes Gabriel pledging to believe in and help Muhammad, with Michael witnessing the pledge. This expresses the honor given to Muhammad ﷺ before his earthly existence. The same account says that his name and obedience are linked with Allah’s command, while making clear that he remains Allah’s servant and messenger.

### Why did Allah take a covenant from the prophets?

The covenant establishes that revelation is one continuous message. Prophets do not compete with or contradict one another. Each confirms the truth brought by the others, and the final messenger is to be recognized and supported by those who receive his message.

### In short

- Allah took a pledge from the prophets to believe in and support a messenger who confirmed their revelation.
- Many explanations identify this final messenger as Muhammad ﷺ, while also emphasizing the prophets’ mutual faith.
- Allah, the prophets, and their communities are witnesses to the covenant.

82.text:
The verse gives the consequence of breaking the covenant: “Whoever turns back after this, they will be the rebellious” (3:82). After Allah has made the pledge clear, abandoning it is a departure from obedience and truth.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Whoever turns back after this”** means turning away after the prophets have accepted the covenant and after its evidence has been established. The person cannot claim that the messenger’s truth was hidden.

An inward reading says this includes abandoning the Prophet’s Sunnah and wandering from his path after his signs and miracles have become clear. The covenant asks for belief and support, not merely an outward statement. It is part of the testimony that leads to Muhammad’s praised station of intercession (17:79).

**“they will be the rebellious”** means that they have left the limits of Allah’s command. They reject the covenant and show disobedience after knowing what they agreed to.

### In short

- The covenant is binding after it has been accepted and witnessed.
- Turning away from the messenger after clear evidence is rebellion.
- The Prophet’s Sunnah and path call believers to remain faithful to Allah’s pledge.

83.text:
The verse challenges those seeking another religion: “Do they desire a way other than Allah’s” (3:83), when every creature submits to Him and all will return to Him? The natural order itself shows that the heavens and earth are under Allah’s command.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Do they desire a way other than Allah’s”** means they seek a religion other than the submission Allah has chosen. The dispute with the People of the Book over Abraham’s religion showed that they rejected the judgment given through revelation. But no one can escape Allah’s authority.

**“knowing that all those in the heavens and the earth submit to His Will”** means all creation is subject to Allah. Believers submit willingly in heart and body. Disbelievers may resist with their beliefs, but their bodies and lives remain under Allah’s power.

The Qur’an says that everything in the heavens and earth prostrates to Allah willingly or unwillingly (13:15). It also describes the shadows of created things inclining in submission and all creatures and angels prostrating (16:48-50). No created being controls its own existence independently.

One report says that when people are asked who created the heavens and earth, they answer, “Allah” (39:38). This admission shows that even those who dispute the faith recognize the Creator’s power.

An inward reading describes a person who looks for a reality other than Allah as chasing a mirage. When the person reaches it, only dust remains. The lights of divine disclosure bring willing submission, while the divine decree overpowers those who resist.

**“willingly or unwillingly”** distinguishes the believer’s conscious submission from the unavoidable submission of creation. The believer obeys by choice. The disbeliever still cannot escape Allah’s command over life, death, and the created world.

**“and to Him they will ˹all˺ be returned”** means everyone will return to Allah after death. He will judge each person according to deeds and distinguish those who submitted willingly from those who rejected the truth.

### What does universal submission teach?

Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās connect the submission of creation with Allah’s covenant and command. The verse points to Allah’s oneness: all beings are under one Creator, whether they acknowledge Him willingly or resist while remaining under His power.

### In short

- No one can escape Allah’s authority over creation.
- Believers submit willingly, while disbelievers remain subject to Allah even when they resist.
- All will return to Allah for judgment.

84.text:
The Prophet is instructed to affirm faith in every revelation: “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us” (3:84). Muslims believe in Allah and all the prophets and scriptures, without rejecting any messenger or dividing revelation into rival communities.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘We believe in Allah’”** declares faith in Allah alone. The Prophet and his community rely on Allah rather than their own strength or power.

**“and what has been revealed to us”** refers to the Qur’an revealed to Muhammad ﷺ. The Muslims accept its teachings and submit to Allah’s guidance.

**“and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants”** includes the revelations given to Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb, and the tribes, al-Asbāṭ, who descended from Yaʿqūb. The wording embraces the children of Israel and the prophets raised among them.

**“and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord”** includes the Torah, the Injīl, and the revelations given to every prophet. The list names several messengers but does not exclude those not named.

**“we make no distinction between any of them”** means Muslims do not believe in some prophets while rejecting others. It does not mean every prophet had the same rank or mission. It means they all came from Allah and their truth is affirmed.

**“and to Him we ˹fully˺ submit”** means that worship and obedience are directed to Allah alone. Submission includes believing in all prophets and following the final message brought by Muhammad ﷺ.

An inward reading says that believers do not attribute faith to their own lower selves, strength, or effort. They believe by Allah’s teaching and guidance. This humility does not remove responsibility. It recognizes that all ability to obey is a gift from Allah. The universal submission of creation provides the setting for this human confession: all in the heavens and earth submit to Allah (13:15), even the shadows and creatures (16:48-50), and the Creator is acknowledged when people are asked who made the heavens and earth (39:38).

The same principle rejects shirk. Muslims do not place one messenger against another or claim that a messenger’s community can reject later revelation. The way of Ibrāhīm, Mūsā, ʿĪsā, and Muhammad is one in its foundation: worship Allah alone and submit to Him.

### How does this faith reflect universal submission?

Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās connect the submission of all creation with Allah’s covenant and command. The believers make that submission conscious by affirming His oneness and accepting the messengers He sent.

### In short

- Muslims believe in Allah and the revelations sent to all the prophets.
- They make no distinction by rejecting some messengers and accepting others.
- Their worship and submission belong to Allah alone.

85.text:
The verse gives a final rule: “Whoever seeks a way other than Islam, it will never be accepted from them” (3:85). All prophets called people to submission to Allah, and the final form of that submission is the religion brought by Muhammad ﷺ.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Whoever seeks a way other than Islam”** means whoever seeks a religion other than submission to Allah. Islam can be used in the general sense of surrendering to Allah, the foundation shared by all prophets. It can also refer specifically to the final Sharīʿah revealed to Muhammad ﷺ.

The earlier prophets and their communities were Muslims in the general sense: they submitted to Allah and followed the revelation given for their time. Their fundamental belief in Allah was the same, though some subsidiary laws differed. When Allah sent a later prophet, the law for that period became the applicable guidance.

After Muhammad ﷺ, al-Muṣṭafā, was sent, Islam means the final religion revealed through him. Earlier laws are no longer independently binding where the final message has replaced them. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid explain the path of submission as the religion Allah has chosen for all people. The final Sharīʿah remains in force until the Day of Judgment. A hadith says that if Mūsā were alive in Muhammad’s time, he would have to follow him. When ʿĪsā returns near the end of the world, he too will follow the law of Muhammad while retaining his prophethood.

**“it will never be accepted from them”** means Allah will not accept a person’s chosen religion if it contradicts the guidance He has sent. This is not because Allah rejects earlier prophets. Rather, it is because accepting all prophets includes following the final messenger when he has come. The Qur’an states that the religion with Allah is Islam (3:19).

**“and in the Hereafter they will be among the losers”** means that those who reject the final guidance lose their share in the Hereafter. The loss is not merely material. It is the loss of salvation and the punishment of the Fire.

An inward reading compares submission to a tree. The Sunnah is its water, faith its fruit, and Allah the one who plants and nurtures it. A deed that does not follow the Prophet’s Sunnah becomes a cause of regret. This image warns that a claim of Islam without following the Prophet’s guidance cannot bear the fruit of faith.

The Qur’an compares a good word to a good tree whose roots are firm and branches reach heaven (14:24-25). The same reading says that Allah expands a person’s breast to Islam with light from the Sunnah (39:22). The Prophet’s way is therefore not an optional decoration. It nourishes the submission and keeps it alive.

Shāfiʿī is reported to have said in a dream that Allah offered him a wish. The allusive account uses this to speak about the gift of submission and the need to follow the Sunnah. The Qur’an also says that all creation submits to Allah (13:15), that creatures and their shadows bow to Him (16:48-50), and that people acknowledge Him as Creator (39:38). It says Allah named the community Muslims (22:78), and it describes the worship of Allah alone as the religion of the prophets. A person should not separate the name Islam from its required obedience.

### What does Islam mean here?

In its broad sense, Islam is submission to Allah, which all prophets taught. In its specific sense, it is the final religion and Sharīʿah given to Muhammad ﷺ. Both meanings lead to the same conclusion: after the final messenger comes, people must accept the guidance Allah has sent through him.

### In short

- Islam means submission to Allah, shared by all prophets and completed in the final message.
- The Sharīʿah of Muhammad ﷺ is the binding guidance after his prophethood.
- Faith must be joined with the Sunnah, whose guidance nourishes submission.

86.text:
The verse asks, “How will Allah guide a people who chose to disbelieve after they had believed” (3:86), even though they had acknowledged the Messenger and received clear proofs? They have chosen wrongdoing after the truth became clear. Allah does not grant them special guidance while they persist in rejecting it.

### How does a person return after apostasy?

The reports distinguish knowingly persisting in disbelief from regretting it and returning to faith. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to say that the man from the Anṣār sought guidance after apostasy, heard the revelation, and returned. A second report from Ibn 'Abbas also describes his return. Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind transmits a related account through Mujāhid. These reports show why the passage warns firmly against apostasy while still describing repentance as a real possibility.

### Phrase by phrase

**“How will Allah guide a people who chose to disbelieve after they had believed”** describes people who first accepted Islam and then returned to disbelief. Their prior faith means that they knew what they were leaving. Ibn 'Abbas reports a case of a man from the Anṣār who embraced Islam, became an idolater again, and later regretted his decision.

The man sent word through his people asking whether the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would accept his repentance. The verses describing the apostasy and later repentance were revealed. When his people recited them to him, he said they were truthful and returned to Islam. The Prophet accepted his repentance. Ibn Jarir, An-Nasaʾī, al-Ḥākim, and Ibn Ḥibbān record the report. Al-Ḥākim says its chain is ṣaḥīḥ, sound.

Another report describes al-Ḥārith bin Suwayd, who had been a Muslim and fought with the Prophet ﷺ, then left Islam and joined his people. When someone read the verses to him, he acknowledged that the reader was truthful, that the Messenger was more truthful, and that Allah is more truthful than all. He returned to Islam and became a good Muslim. Ibn 'Abbas said that the man from the Anṣār returned after hearing the revelation, and a related account transmitted through Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind also recounts a return from apostasy.

**“acknowledged the Messenger to be true”** means they had already testified that Muhammad ﷺ brought the truth. Their later rejection is not simply a lack of familiarity with his message.

**“and received clear proofs”** means that evidence had come to them. The Prophet’s truth was made clear through revelation and signs. They knowingly turned back from what they had recognized.

**“For Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people”** means that Allah does not grant special guidance to those who persist in wrongdoing. It does not mean that repentance is impossible. The next verses explicitly allow repentance and amendment. The warning describes their condition while they continue in rejection, not an unchangeable barrier against returning to faith.

A reflective explanation says that those who have turned away from sincere service cannot expect closeness while remaining in their chosen error. Yet the report of the man from the Anṣār shows that when he regretted his apostasy and returned, Allah accepted him.

### In short

- Some people accepted Islam and later apostatized after recognizing the Messenger’s truth.
- The report of the man from the Anṣār shows that sincere repentance can be accepted.
- Allah does not guide those who persist in wrongdoing, but the next verse makes room for return.

87.text:
The verse describes the consequence of knowingly turning away: “Their reward is that they will be condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity” (3:87). The punishment is expressed as a curse, meaning distance from Allah’s mercy and condemnation by His creation.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Their reward is”** introduces the consequence for people who reject the truth after clear evidence and remain in that state. It is not a reward of honor but a fitting recompense for their choice.

**“they will be condemned by Allah”** means they are distanced from His mercy while they persist in disbelief. One inward reading says their final state follows from the rejection they chose at the beginning and the turning away from service that followed.

**“the angels”** are also described as condemning them. The verse presents their rejection as a matter known beyond human society.

**“and all of humanity”** means that the condemnation is not limited to the believers who witnessed the apostasy. It extends to people who recognize the truth and to the broader community of humankind.

In the reported case of the man from the Anṣār, Ibn 'Abbas is reported to say that the verses were revealed after he asked whether he could repent. The story shows that the warning concerns those who continue in rejection. When the man returned sincerely, he was accepted. An inward interpretation describes the curse as al-Ṭard, expulsion from mercy. This curse is not placed upon everyone who once committed apostasy and later repents.

### In short

- Persistent rejection after clear evidence brings condemnation.
- The curse describes distance from Allah’s mercy.
- The person who sincerely repents is not excluded from forgiveness.

88.text:
The verse says, “They will be in Hell forever” (3:88). Those who persist in rejection will not have their punishment lightened or delayed. The warning describes the final outcome of those who die without repentance.

### Phrase by phrase

**“They will be in Hell forever”** refers to the lasting punishment of those who remain in disbelief. Another explanation connects the pronoun with the curse itself, which is the distance from Allah’s mercy that the previous verse described.

**“Their punishment will not be lightened”** means the suffering will not be reduced, even for a short time. They will not be granted relief from the consequence of knowingly rejecting the truth.

**“nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺”** means they will receive no reprieve or postponement once the punishment is due. The phrase ʿanhum means “from them,” emphasizing that no pause is granted to those being punished. Some commentators say the wording also points to the curse mentioned in the preceding verse. The verse emphasizes the seriousness of the choice to persist in disbelief.

This warning follows the mention of condemnation by Allah, the angels, and humanity. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to say that the man who returned to faith was not among those who remain under the curse. The phrase ʿanhum means “from them.” The verse says that “lā yufattar ʿanhum al-ʿadhāb” means their punishment does not pause or ease for them. It describes the final state of those who remain in disbelief, while the next verse explains that repentance and reform change a person’s outcome.

### In short

- Those who die persisting in disbelief face lasting punishment.
- Their punishment will not be reduced or postponed.
- The next verse distinguishes them from those who repent and amend their conduct.

89.text:
The verse makes clear that the door remains open: “As for those who repent afterwards and mend their ways” (3:89), Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. A person who returns from disbelief and follows repentance with righteous action may be forgiven.

### Phrase by phrase

**“As for those who repent afterwards”** refers to people who turn back to Allah after apostasy or wrongdoing. Ibn 'Abbas reports that the man from the Anṣār asked whether Allah would accept his return, and he became Muslim again when the verses reached him. The report lets us say that the warning in the preceding verses does not close the door to a sincere return.

**“and mend their ways”** means they correct their conduct and sincerely return to Allah’s oneness. Repentance is more than regret in words. It includes leaving disbelief and living according to the faith one has accepted.

**“then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”** means Allah forgives those who sincerely repent and shows them mercy. The report about al-Ḥārith bin Suwayd also describes a man who returned to Islam and became a good Muslim.

An inward reading says that the people reached by mercy were not in the final group of those who remain in rejection, even if others thought they would be. Allah knows who sincerely returns.

### In short

- Repentance is possible after disbelief.
- Returning to Allah must be joined with correcting one’s actions.
- Allah forgives and shows mercy to those who sincerely return.

90.text:
The verse warns about people “who disbelieve after having believed then increase in disbelief” (3:90). Their repentance is not accepted if they keep increasing in rejection until death. They have strayed from the path of truth.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Indeed, those who disbelieve after having believed”** refers to people who first accepted Islam and later rejected it. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās describes people who accepted Islam, apostatized, returned, and then apostatized again. Their situation is not the same as a person who regrets and makes a sincere return.

**“then increase in disbelief”** means they persist in rejection and become more committed to it. Some explanations say this concerns people who accepted Mūsā (Moses), then rejected ʿĪsā (Jesus) and the Injīl (Gospel), and then rejected Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur’an. Abū al-ʿĀliyah says it concerns Jews and Christians who knew the descriptions of Muhammad but continued to disbelieve in him. ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and al-Ḥasan also explain the verse in connection with rejection of Jesus and the Gospel followed by rejection of the final messenger. The attribution to Abu'l- Aliyah makes the point that knowledge of a messenger’s signs does not by itself produce faith if a person continues to turn away. Some say the verse addresses repeated apostasy more generally, so its warning includes anyone who persists in disbelief after faith.

**“their repentance will never be accepted”** means that a last-minute claim of repentance at the point of death does not undo a life of increasing rejection. Another verse says repentance is not accepted from those who continue evil until death is facing them (4:18). This does not contradict the previous verse, which accepts sincere repentance made before that point.

A hadith recorded by al-Bazzār from Ibn ʿAbbās describes people who repeatedly entered Islam and then left it. Their question about repentance led to the revelation of these verses. The account is a warning not to treat repeated rejection as harmless or assume that a person can postpone return until the last moment.

An inward reading applies the verse to people who leave the path of spiritual striving and return to habitual desires. They become more isolated in their darkness and no longer feel regret for the moments of sincere service they have lost. It says that a person who turns away from the Ṭarīq, the path, must feel remorse and return before the heart grows accustomed to estrangement.

The Qur’an says that Allah may turn hearts and eyes away when people refuse to believe at the first opportunity (6:110). The warning is not that Allah rejects a sincere person who turns back. It is that repeatedly choosing disbelief can harden the heart until the person no longer seeks repentance.

### When is repentance no longer accepted?

The verse concerns people who remain in disbelief and continue increasing in it, especially those who wait until death to claim repentance. The previous verse offers forgiveness to those who turn back and amend their conduct while they can still do so.

### In short

- Persistent disbelief after faith leads a person farther from the truth.
- Repentance at the point of death is not the same as sincere return before then.
- The verse urges people to repent while they can still change their course.

91.text:
The verse declares that “if each of those who disbelieve then die as disbelievers were to offer a ransom of enough gold to fill the whole world, it would never be accepted from them” (3:91). After death, wealth cannot purchase release from punishment, and no helper can rescue them.

### Phrase by phrase

**“Indeed, if each of those who disbelieve then die as disbelievers”** describes people who persist in rejection until death. Their final state is different from that of those who repent and return before death.

**“were to offer a ransom of enough gold to fill the whole world”** means that even the greatest imaginable fortune would not pay for forgiveness. The Qur’an says that no compensation will be accepted on that Day (2:123), that a ransom cannot rescue those who die in disbelief (5:36), and that there will be no bargaining or friendship that saves them (14:31). Their wealth and influence cannot change Allah’s judgment.

The same warning appears in a hadith about a person from the Fire. Allah asks whether he would ransom himself with the earth full of gold. He says yes, but Allah tells him that he had been asked in worldly life to do something easier and did not do it. Aḥmad records the report from Anas. The contrast is between an impossible ransom after death and the opportunity to obey Allah while alive.

A report also describes ʿAbd Allāh bin Judʿān, who was generous to guests, helped people in debt, and fed the poor. The Prophet ﷺ was asked whether those good deeds would benefit him. He said they would not, because the man had not believed or asked Allah to forgive him. Good conduct has value, but it cannot replace faith in Allah.

Another report from Aḥmad speaks of a man from Paradise who asks to return to the world and be killed in Allah’s cause ten times because of the honor of martyrdom. A man from the Fire, when offered the whole earth in gold as ransom, accepts, but Allah says he had refused an easier command during his life. The report says that the Hereafter is not a place where people can buy back the chances they refused. It also says that this life is the time to obey, repent, and believe.

**“it would never be accepted from them”** means that the ransom cannot cancel the punishment. The offer fails not because of its size but because the person died without faith and repentance.

**“It is they who will suffer a painful punishment”** means that their outcome is severe and real. It is not a temporary inconvenience that can be exchanged for wealth.

**“and they will have no helpers”** means no one can shield them from the punishment or intercede without Allah’s permission. Wealth, family, and former status cannot rescue them.
